What are the options for a quick Perinton sale?

A Perinton owner can list, sell privately or take a direct cash offer, and a cash route is worth pricing if the house needs work or the owner needs to close soon. The town just finished a townwide revaluation, so a new assessment sits on every parcel and buyers will read it closely.

Perinton is in eastern Monroe County about 10 miles southeast of Rochester. Local paperwork runs through the town's Assessment Office and Building and Codes Department, both at Town Hall on Turk Hill Road, and deeds are recorded by the Monroe County Clerk in Rochester.

What is Perinton and how did it grow?

The town was established in 1812 and covers 34.56 square miles. Its neighbors are East Rochester, Victor, Macedon, Pittsford and Penfield, and its southern line is the Ontario County border. The Village of Fairport sits inside the town on the Erie Canal, and the hamlets include Egypt in the east and Bushnell's Basin in the southwest, where Richardson's Canal House has been on the National Register of Historic Places since 1980.

Settlement began in 1793, when Glover Perrin and his family arrived. Canal and railroad access made Fairport an industrial port from the 1850s, home to firms such as the American Can Company. Outside the village the town stayed rural until the 1950s, and suburban subdivisions now surround the remaining farms. Perinton calls itself a Trail Town USA and maintains the 35-mile Crescent Trail, along with Egypt Park, Perinton Park, Powder Mills Park and Garnsey Arboretum.

What do the Census numbers say about Perinton homes?

The Census Bureau counted 47,479 people in 2020 and estimates 46,823 for July 1, 2025, a change of negative 1.4 percent. The 2020 to 2024 survey gives these housing facts:

  • Owner-occupied rate: 79.2 percent.
  • Median owner-occupied home value: $310,200.
  • Median gross rent: $1,349.
  • Median household income: $112,093, across 20,347 households.
  • Residents 65 or older: 23.8 percent.
  • Bachelor's degree or higher: 62.8 percent.

Nearly a quarter of residents are 65 or older, so a good share of Perinton sales come from retirees who are moving, downsizing or settling an estate. Those sellers often value a firm closing date over the highest possible price.

What changed in the 2026 Perinton revaluation?

The town updated every assessment because the last full update came in 2018 and its equalization rate had slid from 100 percent to 57 percent. The Assessment Office says a revaluation does not raise the total tax collected. It changes how the same levy is divided, and the new values first show up on the 2026 to 2027 tax bills.

Perinton revaluation figures published by the Assessment Office
MeasureResult
Preliminary assessment notices mailed18,234
Informal reviews completed2,152 (11.8 percent)
Applications to the Board of Assessment Review819

If you bought or sold on the old values, compare the new assessment to what comparable houses closed at before you set a price.

How do I contest a Perinton assessment?

Taxes cannot be grieved, but the assessment can. Grievance Day for the next cycle is Tuesday, May 25, 2027, and applications are accepted from May 1 until 8:00 p.m. that day. A mailed form must arrive by the deadline regardless of its postmark.

  • File New York form RP-524, with all four pages completed and signed.
  • Send the original and five copies of the form and the supporting papers.
  • Attach evidence: a closing statement, a listing history, comparable sales, an appraisal or construction costs.
  • Income property needs at least three years of income and expense data.

You do not have to appear in person. Decisions are mailed on or before July 1. After that, the final roll sets the school tax bill for September 1, the town and county bill for January 1 and any village bill for June 1.

What should a Perinton seller review before listing?

The assessment cycle gives a rough timeline. The Assessment Office inspects new construction, remodeling and demolitions from July 1 through March 1, and informal reviews open each October 1. The tentative roll is filed May 1 and the final roll July 1, so a sale in late spring happens while next year's number is still being argued.

  • Read your preliminary assessment notice and compare it with recent sales on the town's sales file.
  • Confirm that every deck, finished basement or addition has a closed permit.
  • Note whether the house is in Fairport village, since a village bill may apply.
  • Gather the deed, payoff statements and your exemption paperwork.

Once those are set, a listing, a private sale and a cash offer can be weighed on the same facts.

Which exemptions apply in Perinton?

Town-administered exemption applications are due March 1. The Assessment Office names these:

  • Senior Citizen.
  • Persons with Disabilities and Limited Income.
  • Veterans.
  • Volunteer Firefighter or Volunteer Ambulance Worker.
  • STAR, which the State administers at tax.ny.gov/star or (518) 457-2036.

Seniors who already hold an exemption are mailed a renewal from June 2026 through January 2027, and each renewal sets an intake appointment. Questions go to the Assessment Office at (585) 223-0770. A buyer should plan to file after closing.

What do Perinton's Building and Codes rules mean for a sale?

Perinton says that work done without a required permit can hold up the sale of a property and can affect an insurance claim. It also warns that the town can issue stop work or cease and desist orders until a permit is obtained. Permits are needed for decks, porches, three-season rooms, finished basements, garages, sheds, fireplaces, generators, fences, hot tubs and pools that hold 24 inches of water or more.

Re-roofing, re-siding, flooring, cabinet installation and replacing windows or doors without enlarging openings usually do not need one. A final inspection leads to a Certificate of Compliance or Occupancy, and the space cannot be used until one is issued. A home business needs both a building permit and a Certificate of Occupancy before it starts. Ask the Building and Codes Department for your address history before listing.

Who covers police, fire and taxes inside Perinton?

The Monroe County Sheriff provides primary law enforcement, and the Village of Fairport has its own police department. Four volunteer fire protection districts split the town: Bushnell's Basin, Egypt, Forest Hills and Perinton. A house inside the village can also carry a village tax bill, so ask where the parcel sits.

Delinquent taxes lead to Monroe County's in rem foreclosure. Action No. 150 covers parcels in Perinton, including the Village of Fairport, and set a public auction for September 11, 2026, a date that has passed. County recording of a deed costs $50 for the first page, and the state taxes the transfer at $2 per $500.

More questions about Perinton, NY

Did Perinton reassess every home recently?

Yes. The town completed a townwide revaluation in 2026, the first since 2018. The Assessment Office mailed 18,234 preliminary notices in March 2026 and says the new values appear on the 2026 to 2027 tax bills.

When is the next Perinton Grievance Day?

May 25, 2027, with filing open from May 1 and a final deadline of 8:00 p.m. that evening. Late or postmark-only mailings will not be reviewed.

Does a revaluation raise my taxes?

Not by itself. The Assessment Office explains that the town's tax levy is set through budgets, so a new assessment only changes how that total is shared. Your bill can rise, fall or stay level depending on how your value compares with others.

Is Fairport the same as Perinton?

No. The Village of Fairport is one part of the town of Perinton, located on the Erie Canal in the northwestern portion. A village tax bill may apply to parcels inside the village.

Can unpermitted work stop a Perinton sale?

It can. The town says work done without a required permit may hold up a sale and complicate insurance claims, and a space cannot be occupied until the Building and Codes Department issues a Certificate of Compliance or Occupancy.

What should Binghamton owners know before putting a house on the market?

Binghamton is the seat of Broome County, and a sale here involves the city for permits, Broome County for tax collection and recording, and a housing market priced well below the rest of New York. The Census Bureau estimates 46,418 residents for July 1, 2025, a drop of 3.1% from the 2020 estimates base.

The Census figures for 2020 to 2024 put the typical owned home at $124,800 and typical rent at $870 a month, and only 44.0% of the 21,393 households own. Most Binghamton households rent rather than own.

The sections below cover the city's setting, how weather and floods affect houses, who bills property tax, which permits matter and what it costs to record a deed in Broome County.

Where is Binghamton and how did it grow?

Binghamton sits in the Southern Tier near the Pennsylvania border, in a valley where the Chenango River meets the Susquehanna. The city covers 10.48 square miles of land, which works out to 4,577.6 people per square mile, and downtown is at about 860 feet while hillside homes climb past 1,800 feet.

The settlement began as Chenango Point and took its name from William Bingham, a Philadelphian who bought the land patent in 1786. It became a village in 1834 and a city in 1867. Canal and railroad connections drew cigar makers and then the Endicott Johnson shoe company. IBM was founded in the greater Binghamton area, and the flight simulator was invented in the city. At its peak, around the mid-1950s, the population was about 85,000.

The old grid laid out near the rivers gives way to curving streets on the Southside hills. Historic districts include the Railroad Terminal Historic District and the Abel Bennett Tract on the West Side, and landmark or historic-district buildings go through design review before demolition.

How do floods and winter weather affect a Binghamton house?

Floods are part of the city's record: major floods hit in 1865, 1935, 1936, 2006 and 2011. After the 1935 and 1936 events the city built flood walls along the Susquehanna and Chenango, and Broome County maintains 17.5 miles of levees, many of them in Binghamton.

  • Expect buyers near the rivers to ask about basement water, sump pumps and any past repairs. Gather receipts before you list.
  • Yearly snowfall averages 86.5 inches, with about 164 days of measurable precipitation, so roof condition, gutters and heating systems get close attention in an inspection.

A house with water damage, an old furnace or a tired roof is a common reason owners here look at selling as-is rather than paying for repairs first.

What does the local economy mean for Binghamton house values?

The region built its wealth on manufacturing and lost much of it after the Cold War, and electronics and defense work has been shrinking since 1990. Education and health care now carry the city. Binghamton University, Broome Community College, United Health Services and Lourdes Hospital are major employers in the area.

The Census figures show the result: median household income of $45,578, per capita income of $30,320 and a poverty rate of 32.6%. About 30.7% of adults 25 and older hold a bachelor's degree. The mean commute is only 19.0 minutes, and 79.8% of residents had the same address a year earlier.

With values this low, a realistic price for your block depends on recent sales nearby, so look at your own street before relying on any citywide figure.

Who collects Binghamton property tax, and how do you contest an assessment?

Broome County collects it. The City Treasurer no longer collects property and school taxes, and the county's tax office also handles in-rem foreclosures, bankruptcies and tax certificates for the city and the Binghamton City School District.

The City Assessor handles assessments. Grievance Day for 2026 was May 26, 2026, and a complaint had to be filed by then on form RP-524 with the city's review board. That deadline has passed, so for 2027 ask the Assessor's Office for the new date and file before it.

If back taxes are the reason you are selling, note that the county runs an installment program for delinquent owners in danger of foreclosure. It requires 25% down and 24 monthly payments at 1% monthly interest, and all new taxes must be paid on time during the plan. A sale that pays the balance at closing ends the problem sooner.

Which permits and housing programs affect a Binghamton sale?

The Building Construction and Code Enforcement office requires a building permit under Section 200-9 of the city code for construction, alteration, removal, demolition and work on electrical, plumbing and HVAC systems. A permit must be on display before work begins.

  • Plumbing work in every kind of occupancy, including one- and two-family homes, must be done by a licensed Master Plumber.
  • Demolition and work that affects a structural element need a permit, and landmark or historic-district buildings go through the Commission on Architecture and Urban Design first.
  • Street work, including a dumpster in the public right of way, needs a separate permit from the Department of Engineering.

The city's First-Time Homebuyer Program gives deferred loans of up to $10,000 for down payment and closing costs. If title to the home is sold or transferred within 5 years, or it stops being the owner's principal residence, the whole loan comes due. After 5 years it is forgiven. If you bought through this program, expect a payoff at closing and ask the Housing Division for the figure.

What are the Broome County recording costs for a Binghamton deed?

Recording happens at the Broome County Clerk's office in the County Office Building on Hawley Street, and the clerk estimates about $190 for a standard two-page residential deed once the state forms are counted. Sellers sign the deed before a notary, and the TP-584 and RP-5217 must be signed by both seller and buyer.

Broome County Clerk fees for a residential deed
ItemFee
Deed$45 plus $5 per page
Transfer tax return (TP-584)$10 filing fee plus tax owed
Real property transfer report (RP-5217)$125 for residential property
Transfer tax in Broome County$5 per $1,000 ($4 state, $1 county)

Source: Broome County Clerk, Deed FAQs. Round an uneven price up to the next $500 before applying the rate, so a $175,100 sale is taxed as $175,500. A seller who lives out of state also completes form IT-2663 for estimated income tax. The clerk's Fraud Alert service emails you when a document is recorded under your name, which is useful once the house is sold.

What choices does a Binghamton seller have?

An agent listing, a private sale and a cash purchase all work here, and the right choice turns on what shape the house is in and how soon you need to close. Listing suits a turnkey single-family home on a quiet block. A cash sale suits a house with flood history, a vacant two-family with code issues, or an inherited property that you would rather not renovate.

Before you accept any figure, pull the assessed value and recent comparable sales, price out the repairs a buyer would ask for, and confirm what, if anything, you owe in back taxes or program loans.

More questions about Binghamton, NY

Where do Binghamton tax payments go?

Pay Broome County's Real Property Tax Services. The county is the collection agent for the City of Binghamton and the Binghamton City School District, so the city treasurer no longer takes tax payments. Mail goes to the county's post office box in Binghamton, and you can also pay in person.

Is Binghamton Grievance Day still open?

No. Grievance Day for 2026 was May 26, 2026, and the filing deadline that day was 4:30 pm. For the next cycle, call the City Assessor's Office for the date and file form RP-524 before it.

What happens to my first-time homebuyer loan if I sell?

The full loan becomes due. Under the city's program, selling or transferring title within 5 years, or moving out of the home, makes 100% repayable. After 5 years the deferred loan is forgiven in full.

How much transfer tax will I pay selling in Binghamton?

Expect $5 per $1,000 of the price in Broome County, rounded up to the next $500. The state takes $4 of that and the county $1. A $120,000 sale produces $600. Houses at $1 million or more add a 1% buyer-paid tax.

Is a permit needed for repairs before I sell my Binghamton house?

Yes, for most structural, electrical, plumbing and HVAC work. Section 200-9 of the city code requires a building permit displayed on site before work starts. Plumbing must be done by a licensed Master Plumber, and historic-district buildings get design review first.

Which sale routes work best when time is short in Mount Pleasant?

Two routes move fast here. One is a listing priced and staged to draw offers within weeks. The other is an as-is purchase by a cash buyer, which concedes some price and removes repairs, open houses and a financing contingency.

Prices in Mount Pleasant sit high: the Census figure for a typical owner-occupied home is $788,900. A roof, a service panel or a permit clean-up at that level can run to tens of thousands, and some owners would rather hand the project to a buyer who wants it.

Either way, begin with the same folder: your deed, a recent Receiver of Taxes bill, the mortgage payoff letter, and permits or occupancy certificates for work done on the property.

Who lives in Mount Pleasant, according to the Census?

Mount Pleasant is both growing and well off. The Census estimate for mid-2025 is 45,444 people, up 2.2 percent on the 2020 base, and owners live in 70.5 percent of homes.

The 2020 to 2024 survey counts 15,312 households with a middle income of $142,857 and rent around $1,941. Degree holders make up 57.1 percent of adults, commutes average 30.9 minutes, and 20.8 percent of residents were born abroad. Full tables are on the Census QuickFacts page for Mount Pleasant.

People buying at this price borrow heavily, and their lenders insist on clean paperwork. Open permits and missing certificates are what most often stall a mortgage closing in town.

How is Mount Pleasant divided into villages and hamlets?

The town occupies central Westchester, roughly 27 miles above Manhattan. It runs from the Hudson River on its west to the Kensico Reservoir and North Castle on its east, with New Castle and Ossining to the north and Greenburgh to the south.

Within those lines are villages and hamlets, and the address decides which name a buyer will use:

  • Sleepy Hollow, once North Tarrytown, is a village in the southwest.
  • Pleasantville is a village in the northeast, and Thornwood lies just south of it.
  • Valhalla, in the southeast, is home to Town Hall.
  • Hawthorne, Pocantico Hills, Scarborough and Archville are hamlets, and part of Briarcliff Manor is inside the town.

The Rockefeller estate Kykuit in Pocantico Hills is a National Historic Landmark. In 2017 county officials unveiled plans for a biotechnology campus of about three million square feet next to Westchester Medical Center in Valhalla. Because so many school systems overlap here, tell buyers which district serves your parcel.

Which school districts and tax dates apply to a Mount Pleasant house?

Eight districts reach into the town: Tarrytown, Mount Pleasant, Pocantico Hills, Valhalla, Pleasantville, Chappaqua, Byram Hills and Briarcliff Manor. The Receiver of Taxes collects for all of them, and your bill shows which one covers your lot.

Mount Pleasant tax calendar and late charges (Town of Mount Pleasant Receiver of Taxes)
BillDueLate charge
County and townApril 302% in May, climbing to 12% January through April
School, first halfSeptember 302% in October, 5% in November, 7% December to January
School, second halfJanuary 3110% in February and March, 12% in April

The Receiver cannot waive a penalty once a deadline passes, and parcels left unpaid for 21 months go to foreclosure. Payments can be made at Town Hall in Valhalla on weekdays from 8:30 to 4:30, by mail with a U.S. postmark, or online, where a card carries a 2.25 percent fee and an electronic check carries none. If a sale closes after the September payment, the January half still comes due, and the town tells sellers to alert the buyer. Write that into the contract.

How do assessments and exemptions work in Mount Pleasant?

Valuation, transfer records and exemptions all run through the Town Assessor. Grievance Day is the third Tuesday of June, and exemption applications close June 1.

  • Informal review requests go in writing by the last business day of March, ahead of the June 1 tentative roll, and none are handled between April 1 and August 1.
  • Available exemptions cover STAR, seniors, veterans, people with disabilities, and volunteer firefighters or ambulance workers.
  • Assessed value divided by the residential assessment ratio gives the office's market value estimate.
  • Send plans, a description of the work and a cost estimate, and the office will say in writing how a renovation might move your assessment.

Buyers should phone the Receiver so bills reach them. Sellers can ask the Assessor which exemptions sit on the parcel before the deed is signed. Forms are posted on the town's Assessor page.

What building-department steps come before a Mount Pleasant closing?

A certificate of occupancy or compliance comes from the Building Department once the permit, fees, final inspection and a notarized Affidavit of Final Cost are done. Electrical work also needs its own certificate.

That chain of steps matters for an aging deck, a finished basement or a new roof. The town's permit list takes in additions, boilers, central air, decks, fences, hot tubs, interior alterations, permanent generators, pools, retaining walls, roofs, solar panels, sheds, storage tanks and stair changes. Unpermitted work blocks the certificate and can bring a stop-work order and fines.

Permit review can take four to six weeks. Since July 1, 2026 filings go through the Online Service Center without paper, and plans must cite the 2025 building code. Oil tanks deserve a mention: removing one takes building and plumbing permits plus inspections, and tanks of 1,100 gallons or more must be registered with the Westchester County Department of Health. Villages sit inside the town, so ask whether your address answers to the town building office or a village office. A buyer paying cash for the house as-is can accept open items, which may spare you the clean-up.

Owners with an unapproved basement apartment or an addition that breaks a setback may need a variance. Accessory apartments, site plans and variances go through Planning and Zoning, a division of the Building Department. A variance applicant submits surveys and plans, publishes the public notice in the Journal News, mails notice to neighboring owners and files at least 15 days before a Zoning Board meeting. That is a lengthy road to take just to sell, so weigh it against a buyer who accepts the house unchanged.

Which office records a Mount Pleasant deed, and what does it charge?

Deeds go to the Westchester County Clerk's Land Records Division. Its schedule starts with a $45 statutory fee, and because Mount Pleasant spans several municipalities, the $0.50 charge for each extra town named can apply to a parcel on a boundary.

The clerk's worked example, a three-page residential deed in one municipality, comes to $190 in fees. State transfer tax is figured on the price rounded up to a multiple of $500, so $404,501 becomes $405,000 and the tax is $1,620, due when the deed is presented. Sales at $1 million or more add a buyer-paid one percent, as the state's transfer tax page explains.

More questions about Mount Pleasant, NY

What are the property tax due dates in Mount Pleasant?

April 30 for town and county tax, then September 30 and January 31 for the two school halves. Penalties start the next month and the Receiver cannot forgive them.

What is the typical home value in Mount Pleasant?

About $788,900 for owner-occupied homes in the Census 2020 to 2024 survey, set against a household income of $142,857 and rent near $1,941.

Does the town require a certificate of occupancy before a sale?

The town issues it when permitted work clears final inspection, and unpermitted work stops it. Mortgage lenders may ask to see it, though a cash purchaser can take the house as it is.

How much do recording fees run in Westchester?

The clerk's example of a three-page residential deed is $190, with extra pages billed separately and transfer tax added.

Who owes the mansion tax in Mount Pleasant?

The buyer, at one percent of a $1 million or higher price on a residence. Sellers are liable only when the buyer fails to pay.

Selling in Lancaster?

Taxes on the sale itself

See the transfer tax guide.

What routes lead to a sale of a Lancaster, NY house?

Three routes lead to a sale in Lancaster: an agent listing, a sale between you and a buyer you find yourself, and a direct cash purchase. Which one fits depends on how soon you need to be done and what shape the building is in. A tidy ranch with no deadline suits a listing. A house with a failing roof, a probate to settle or a tenant who will not leave tends to suit a quick, as-is buyer.

  • Agent listing: wide exposure, with showings, a lender's appraisal and the chance a buyer's financing falls through.
  • Owner-handled sale: you set price and terms, and your attorney drafts the contract and deed.
  • Cash purchase: no repair requests and no mortgage contingency, since the buyer takes the property in its present state.

Every route ends the same way in Lancaster: a notarized deed, transfer tax forms for the Erie County Clerk, and settlement of whatever tax is still owed on the parcel.

Where is Lancaster, and what is it like for homeowners?

Lancaster sits in Erie County, roughly 11 miles east of downtown Buffalo, on about 37 square miles with two villages inside its borders, Lancaster and Depew. According to the town's history page, it was carved out of Clarence by the State Legislature in 1833, the Village of Lancaster incorporated in 1849, and Depew followed in 1894. Five major railroads once crossed the town, and the rail lines are still active.

Residents numbered 45,075 in the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate, nearly identical to the 45,106 counted in 2020. The Town tax office says five school districts bill Lancaster addresses: Lancaster Central, Depew Union Free, Alden Central, Clarence Central and Iroquois Central. Most of the town falls in Lancaster Central, yet the district printed on your tax bill is the one to quote to buyers.

Getting around is easy by car. The Thruway (I-90) crosses the north end, NY 33 runs just below it, US 20 follows Broadway through the middle, and NY 78 (Transit Road) forms the western edge. East of Bowen Road the town is still filling in and keeps a more rural feel.

Heritage counts for something in the village. Twelve Lancaster buildings are on the National Register of Historic Places, eleven of them along Broadway in the Village of Lancaster Historic District and one, the Hull House on Genesee Street, in the town. The Building Department's page carries a Village of Lancaster historic preservation application, so owners near Broadway should ask the village what review applies before promising a buyer a facade or window project.

How do Lancaster home values and household figures compare?

The middle owner-occupied home in Lancaster is valued at $277,600, with about four in five homes lived in by their owners. That gives you a rough anchor, though a survey median cannot price an individual house, so ask for recent nearby sales before you settle on a number. The profile below draws on the Census Bureau's Lancaster town profile.

The town counts 19,722 households, and 22.1% of its residents have reached 65. A short 20-minute average commute is one of the quieter selling points for a house here.

Will the Lancaster Building Department care about my past renovations?

It can, because the Building Department enforces the state building and fire code, zoning, stormwater practices and flood plain rules across both the town and the village. The department's page says that nobody may build, alter, move or demolish a structure without first obtaining a permit.

Applications are posted for decks, fences, pools and hot tubs, sheds, signs, demolition and one- and two-family dwellings, along with a handout on as-built survey requirements. If a deck, an addition or a finished basement was added before you bought, ask the office whether the project is on file and was signed off. A clear answer saves negotiating time later.

  • Inspections tied to a permit are booked by phone with the office, which keeps weekday hours.
  • The department also links resources on vacant and "zombie" properties, handy for an inherited house that has sat empty.
  • Truck routes and yard sale permits are separate matters handled through the town and its Highway Department.

What are the Lancaster tax deadlines, and what happens to late payments?

Town and County bills are due February 15 and school bills October 15, pushed back a day if the date lands on a weekend or holiday. The Town's tax office, which sits inside the Town Clerk's office, collects both. A mailed check is on time only when the postmark carries the due date or an earlier one, and the office states there are no exceptions.

School tax picks up a 7.5% penalty for the rest of October and 9% through November. Whatever is unpaid after November 30 goes onto the Erie County tax roll. Town and County penalties begin at 1.5% in the first two weeks late and reach 7.5% by the end of April, and interest runs after that.

The town office takes Town and County payments through June 30 and school payments through November 30. Past those dates, payments and payoff questions go to Erie County Real Property Tax Services in Buffalo. Interest changes the payoff monthly, so request a county figure before fixing a closing date.

What will the Erie County Clerk charge on a Lancaster deed?

Erie County adds its own transfer tax to the state's, for a combined $4.50 per $500 of price, split $2.00 state and $2.50 county, and the seller is responsible for it. The Clerk's deed page rounds the price up to the next $500, so a sale at Lancaster's $277,600 median value would owe about $2,502.

Recording adds a $45 statutory fee, $5 for each page, $10 to file the TP-584 and $125 to file the RP-5217 report for residential property. The deed itself must carry original signatures, a notary's acknowledgment, a full legal description and street addresses for every party, since P.O. boxes are rejected.

  • An owner aged 62 or older who has lived in a one- or two-family house for a year or more can claim the reduced $2.00-per-$500 rate.
  • Residential sales at $1 million or above add a 1% mansion tax that the buyer pays.
  • The Clerk also asks for a Notice of Sale or Transfer of Ownership on residential property.

State guidance on the Tax Department's transfer tax page sets the TP-584 and payment at 15 days after delivery of the deed. Afterward, close out your STAR registration through the state's STAR page, and let the new owner register for the credit.

More questions about Lancaster, NY

Which office collects tax on a Lancaster property?

The Lancaster tax office, part of the Town Clerk's office, collects Town, County and school bills. Later payments, after June 30 for Town and County or November 30 for school, go to Erie County Real Property Tax Services in Buffalo.

Does Lancaster belong to one school district?

No. Lancaster Central covers most of it, yet Depew Union Free, Alden Central, Clarence Central and Iroquois Central also bill Lancaster addresses, per the Town tax office. Read your own tax bill to see which one applies.

Who covers transfer tax on a Lancaster sale?

The seller covers the state and Erie County transfer tax when the deed reaches the County Clerk. The total is $4.50 per $500, and qualifying owners aged 62 and over may pay a reduced $2.00 rate.

Must I get a permit before listing my Lancaster house?

A plain sale does not appear among the permit triggers. The Building Department's rule covers building, altering, moving and demolishing, so use a call to the office to confirm that earlier decks, pools or additions were permitted and closed out.

Is a damaged Lancaster house still sellable?

Yes. You can market it as-is to investors, list it and price in the repairs, or take cash from a buyer who purchases without a repair list. Check with the Building Department about open permits before accepting any offer.

You can list it with an agent, sell it yourself, or sell for cash to a buyer who takes the house as it stands. In Freeport, a village on Long Island's South Shore, each route runs through the same village offices, Nassau County recording and New York State transfer tax rules.

With a median owner-occupied home value of $505,900, Freeport sales involve enough money that closing costs, flood questions and unpermitted work can each move the final number. Sorting those items out before a buyer's attorney finds them is usually the fastest way to a closing date.

What do the Census figures show about Freeport housing?

Freeport is a family-oriented village with a high owner-occupancy rate and larger households than most of New York. Its median home value sits well above the state's upstate cities, and rents are high too.

If you are working with a buyer or attorney, make sure all disclosures and contracts are explained in a language you read comfortably.

Where is Freeport and what is it known for?

Freeport lies inside the Town of Hempstead in Nassau County. At the 2020 census its 44,472 residents made it the second largest village in the state. It covers about 4.6 square miles, and Sunrise Highway (Route 27) cuts across it from west to east while the Meadowbrook State Parkway marks its eastern edge.

Settlement goes back to the 1640s. Voters chose the name Freeport in 1853 and incorporated the village on October 18, 1892. The village started a municipal electric utility in 1898, and that utility still runs. Oystering gave way to commuting, and canals such as the Woodcleft Canal, home of the Nautical Mile restaurant strip, reach the Great South Bay.

  • Rail: the Long Island Rail Road reaches Manhattan in roughly 45 minutes.
  • Schools: Freeport Public Schools runs eight schools, with one high school.
  • Waterfront: boat access and canal frontage give many homes a marine setting, along with a flood obligation.

How does flood zone status affect a Freeport home sale?

For a large share of homes in the southern part of the village, flood zone status is part of the sale. The village flood management page explains that a premises may lie in or beside a FEMA special flood hazard area, and it states that a regular homeowners policy does not cover flood damage. A mortgage holder in a flood zone must carry a separate flood policy.

Freeport takes part in the National Flood Insurance Program and reports a 10% discount on flood premiums. Its Building Department keeps elevation certificates on file and has a certified floodplain manager on staff.

  • Ask the Building Department whether an elevation certificate exists for your address.
  • Look up the flood zone and base flood elevation on FEMA's site or through the village.
  • Remember the substantial improvement rule: if repairs or additions cost 50% or more of a building's market value, the building has to meet new construction standards.

What permit and code checks matter before listing in Freeport?

The village Building Department administers building, plumbing, electrical and housing codes, and it also regulates multiple residences and unsafe buildings. Permit filings now go through the village's OpenGov portal, and structural applications need signed and sealed plans.

A buyer's attorney can ask for proof that finished basements, extensions or extra kitchens were permitted. If something was built without a permit, resolve it before listing so the question does not surface mid-contract.

  • Pull your permit history from the Building Department at 46 N Ocean Avenue.
  • Confirm that any converted space has the proper approvals.
  • Check the village zoning map if the house holds more than one unit.

Which village services and exemptions go with a Freeport house?

The village runs more of its own services than most Long Island communities. Its departments include the Assessor, Building, Electric, Water, Public Works, Fire, Police and Recreation, and the Treasurer oversees both the Treasurer's Office and the Tax Office. The Village Clerk handles licenses, permits and village records and works with the Planning Board and Zoning Board.

A seller should tell the buyer which village services attach to the property and confirm what is billed separately.

  • Electric: Freeport operates its own electric department, and its rates and project bids are posted on the village electric site.
  • Water and sewer: the Water Department publishes rates and fees, a conservation and regulations page and an annual water quality report.
  • Sanitation: Public Works posts a pickup schedule by area, so the collection day depends on the street.
  • Emergency alerts: Emergency Management lists hurricane evacuation routes and a CivicReady alert sign-up.

Exemptions listed by the Assessor include senior citizens, veterans, limited income disability, clergy, home improvement, non-profit, business development and volunteer firefighters and ambulance workers, plus the STAR program. Ask the Assessor how a change of ownership affects any exemption you hold.

What are the village tax dates, and who records the deed?

Freeport residents pay a village tax separate from Town of Hempstead, county and school levies. The village Assessor's page lists its own calendar, and Nassau County runs a different assessment calendar, so call the county for its dates.

  • January 1: village final assessment roll published; the first village bill is due between March 1 and March 31.
  • September 1 to 30: second-half village bills are payable without penalty.
  • October 1: deadline for exemption applications and the taxable status date, by 4:30 p.m. in person.
  • November 1 to the third Tuesday in November: grievance window, closing at 8 p.m.

The deed itself is recorded by the Nassau County Clerk, who keeps the official index of real property ownership and offers online land record search. New York's transfer tax is $2 per $500 of price, paid by the seller on a standard sale and reported on Form TP-584 filed with the recording office.

More questions about Freeport, NY

Does a Freeport seller pay the New York transfer tax?

Yes, on an ordinary sale the seller pays $2 for each $500 of the price, and the TP-584 form goes to the county clerk with the deed. The separate 1% tax on residences of $1 million or more lands on the buyer.

Will flood zone status delay my Freeport closing?

It can if the buyer's lender wants flood insurance quotes first. Collect your flood zone, elevation certificate and any claim history early so the buyer can price a policy without waiting.

Where do I get a permit record for my Freeport house?

Ask the village Building Department, which handles permits and keeps elevation certificates. Its office is at 46 N Ocean Avenue, and permit filings now run through the village OpenGov system.

When must I file a grievance on a Freeport assessment?

The village window runs from November 1 until 8 p.m. on the third Tuesday in November, and the application has to be physically in the Assessor's Office by then. A postmark does not count.

Is Freeport its own tax collector?

Partly. The village bills its own tax, and Town of Hempstead, Nassau County and school district taxes arrive separately. Ask the village Treasurer and the county for payoff figures before you close.

Does Freeport have its own electric service?

Yes. The village Electric Department supplies power and posts rates and bid notices. The village history dates the municipal utility to 1898, and Freeport is one of two municipally owned electric systems in Nassau County.

What are a Cortlandt seller's choices, and when does cash make sense?

Selling in Cortlandt means weighing an agent listing against a private sale or a cash purchase of the house as-is. Cash tends to make sense when the property needs work, the owner is behind on payments or taxes, an estate must be wrapped up, or a closing date cannot slip.

A listing can stall while a seller pays for repairs before the first showing. A cash buyer accepts the house with its flaws and quotes accordingly, which is why the offer comes in below a polished listing. Put both numbers beside the payoff on your mortgage, any unpaid tax and the costs you would pay at closing.

  • A direct sale to someone you know suits owners who are comfortable with contracts.
  • A cash sale suits a home with deferred maintenance, an inheritance, a tenant dispute or a looming tax penalty.

Where is Cortlandt, and how does its geography affect a house?

Cortlandt sits in the northwestern corner of Westchester County. The Hudson River and the City of Peekskill bound it on the west, Putnam County's Philipstown and Putnam Valley on the north, Yorktown on the east and New Castle and Ossining on the south. The town was incorporated in 1788, covers 50 square miles in all and holds nearly 11 square miles of water, about a fifth of its area.

It contains the incorporated villages of Buchanan and Croton-on-Hudson and hamlets including Cortlandt Manor, Montrose, Crugers and Verplanck, along with neighborhoods such as Mount Airy, Oscawana and Van Cortlandtville. US Route 9 follows the river, the eastern end of the Bear Mountain Bridge lands here, and Metro-North serves the Cortlandt and Croton-Harmon stations, with Amtrak also stopping at Croton-Harmon. In 1781 George Washington's army crossed the Hudson at King's Ferry, between Verplanck's Point and Stony Point.

The Census Bureau counted 42,545 residents in 2020 and estimates 42,413 for July 1, 2025.

Which school districts and village lines apply to a Cortlandt address?

The Tax Receiver collects for five school districts: Croton-Harmon, Hendrick Hudson, Lakeland, Putnam Valley and Yorktown. A Cortlandt address can therefore mean very different school taxes for houses a few miles apart. Name the district in any listing or offer packet, because buyers sort by it.

Village boundaries add another layer. The villages of Buchanan and Croton-on-Hudson levy their own village taxes, and those are billed separately from the Town and County bill. If you sell a house inside a village, ask the village office for its bill and its collection dates as well. The Tax Receiver's office page links to both villages for that purpose.

When do Cortlandt tax bills fall due, and what are the penalties?

Westchester towns act as collection agents, so the Cortlandt Tax Receiver bills Town, County and school taxes. The Town and County bill goes out by April 1 and is due April 30. The school bill goes out by September 1 and can be paid in full by September 30 or in two halves, the first by September 30 and the second by January 31.

  • Town and County penalty: 2% in May, 5% in June and July, 7% in August and September, 10% from October to December and 12% from January to April.
  • School first half: 2% in October, 5% in November, 7% in December and January, 10% in February and March, 12% in April.
  • Penalties cannot be waived by any Town employee.
  • Prior-year taxes unpaid by June 30 become a lien on July 1, and a property with taxes unpaid after 21 months can be foreclosed.

The office bills over 15,000 parcels and collects more than $188 million a year. It is at 1 Heady Street in Cortlandt Manor, open weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. and on the last Saturday of April and September from 9 a.m. to noon. A drop box in the courtyard takes after-hours payments, no cash. Online payment adds a $1.00 fee for e-check or a 1.81% third-party fee for cards. Mail payments need a United States postmark on or before the due date, since postage meter marks do not count.

How do assessments, exemptions and grievances work in Cortlandt?

Cortlandt runs on a different calendar than most upstate towns. May 1 is tax status day, which is also the exemption and tax map change deadline. The tentative roll is published June 1, Grievance Day is the third Tuesday in June, and the final roll appears September 15. This year's Grievance Day was June 16, 2026. The 2027 date is Tuesday, June 15.

The Assessor's office says the prior year's final roll sets the current year's taxes, so the 2022 roll was used to print the 2023 to 2024 bills. A grievance is a challenge to the assessment, not the tax itself, and the Town suggests you ask whether you could actually sell for the full market value shown. Form RP-524 must be filed with the Assessment Office even if you plan to appear before the Board, and a mailed copy must arrive by 8 p.m. on Grievance Day.

Senior citizen and disability with limited income exemptions renew every year: the Assessor mails renewal forms in February and wants them back with supporting papers by May 1. If you are selling a house that carries one of these exemptions, tell the buyer that the benefit belongs to the owner and has to be applied for again after the sale.

Three recent changes are worth noting. Enhanced STAR no longer has an application, because the state verifies income yearly. The Town took over the Village of Croton's assessing function after the village gave it up in 2025. And a new exemption for veterans with a permanent and total disability rating needs local adoption: the Town scheduled a public hearing for November 17, 2026, the county and Croton had already adopted it, and the filing deadline would be May 1, 2027.

What do deeds and state transfer taxes look like for a Cortlandt sale?

Westchester County Clerk's Land Records Division records deeds, mortgages and satisfactions, and it takes electronic filings. Cover pages, Form TP-584 transfer tax returns and RP-5217 reports must be created through the clerk's PREP portal. Deeds go back to 1680 in its online search.

State transfer tax is $2 for each $500 of consideration, ordinarily paid by the seller, with the return and payment due no later than 15 days after the deed is delivered. On a price of $1 million or more, a separate 1% additional tax applies to the buyer. For permits and any open violations, start with the Town and, for village addresses, the village hall.

More questions about Cortlandt, NY

Does a Cortlandt house need repairs before it can be sold for cash?

No. A cash buyer takes the property as-is and prices in the work. Expect the offer to be lower than a repaired listing, and check for open permits or violations first.

When is the next Grievance Day in Cortlandt?

Tuesday, June 15, 2027. Grievance Day is the third Tuesday in June, and 2026's date, June 16, has passed. Exemption applications are due May 1.

Who collects property taxes in Cortlandt?

The Cortlandt Tax Receiver collects Town, County and school taxes at 1 Heady Street. Buchanan and Croton-on-Hudson bill their own village taxes separately.

What happens if I miss the April 30 Town and County tax date?

A 2% penalty applies in May, rising to 5% in June and July. The Town cannot waive it, so pay as soon as you can.

Where is a Cortlandt deed recorded?

At the Westchester County Clerk's Land Records Division in White Plains. File Form TP-584 with it, and build the cover page in the clerk's PREP portal.

How is the Town of Haverstraw laid out?

The town covers 27.41 square miles, but 5.26 of them are water, and it stretches across Rockland County's northern section from the Hudson River to the western county line. The village of Haverstraw holds the historic downtown, and part of Harriman State Park, including Lake Sebago, Lake Welch and Lake Kanawauke, lies in the west of the town.

Settlers took the name from the Dutch Haverstroo, oat straw, which described the riverside grasslands; a land purchase from local natives in 1666 was confirmed as a patent in 1671. About a fifth of the town's area is water, so a parcel near the river or a lake deserves a look at its drainage and flood history before you pick an asking price.

The Haverstraw-Stony Point Central School District is the one the Town of Haverstraw names in its tax collection notice, with parcels inside it eligible for installment payment of school tax. What penalties apply to late Haverstraw tax payments?

Town and county tax is collected from January 1 through January 31 without penalty, and the Town of Haverstraw, a town of the first class, adds 1% in February and 2% in March. On April 1, unpaid tax is turned over to Rockland County Finance.

  • Installments: bills above $50 may be paid in four parts, with a 5% service charge and the first part due by January 31.
  • Later parts: April 15, July 15 and October 15, paid to the Rockland County Commissioner of Finance in Pomona.
  • March payments: after March 15, checks must be bank or certified checks, in the office by close of business on March 31, with no postmarks accepted.
  • Cards: accepted, with a 2.45% convenience fee charged by the card provider.

Elderly or disabled owner-occupants of one-, two- or three-family homes can ask the Receiver of Taxes for third-party notification on form RP-923. A seller closing mid-year should ask the closing attorney which installment has been paid, so the proration comes out right.

What permits should a Haverstraw seller check?

The town Building Department issues building permits and Certificates of Occupancy and points owners to section 84-4 of the Town Code to see which repairs and construction need them. Those documents show that a house meets the codes for structural soundness and fire safety.

Before you list, confirm that every addition, finished basement and converted space has a permit and a Certificate of Occupancy on file. The department also handles questions about fire permits, burning permits, fire inspections and sprinkler systems.

How do the deed and transfer tax work for a Haverstraw sale?

Haverstraw deeds go to the Rockland County Clerk, whose land records page requires originals in recordable form, legible, signed and notarized. State transfer tax runs $2 per $500 of the price, rounded up, so the $387,500 Census median value would owe $1,550, usually from the seller.

The state tax return and payment are due by the 15th day after the deed is delivered, and the clerk takes them when the deed is recorded. A buyer owes a 1% mansion tax on a residence at $1 million or more. The clerk's land records page offers downloadable forms for the most common filings.

What happens to unpaid Haverstraw taxes after March?

Rockland County Finance takes over collection of unpaid bills on April 1. Until then the Receiver of Taxes adds 1% in February and 2% in March, and late-March checks must be certified or bank checks.

No. The 2026 filing window ran from May 1 through May 28. Grievance Day falls on the fourth Tuesday in May each year, so the next chance is spring 2027.

Yes, if the bill is over $50, with a 5% service charge and the first part due by January 31. Later parts fall on April 15, July 15 and October 15, so ask your attorney which have been paid before closing.

The Rockland County Clerk, which accepts only original, legible, signed and notarized documents. The transfer tax return goes in within 15 days after the deed is delivered.

Where is Valley Stream and how did its housing develop?

Valley Stream lies in the Town of Hempstead along the Queens border and covers about 3.5 square miles at only 16 feet above sea level. The name comes from Valley Stream Brook, and Robert Pagan, the farmer who became the first postmaster, chose it for the community. The Post Office accepted the name in 1843. Growth followed the railroad and Merrick Road. In 1922 a developer built homes on avenues such as Avondale, Berkeley and Cambridge, and the Gibson station opened in 1929. The village counted 11,790 residents in 1930 and passed 38,000 by 1960, so much of the housing dates from that burst of building.

It depends on the street. Most of the village falls in the Valley Stream elementary districts 13, 24 and 30, which share the Valley Stream Central High School District. Some southern blocks are zoned instead to the Hewlett-Woodmere Union Free School District.

Buyers ask about schools first, so confirm the district for your address before listing and say which one applies. The same address also decides which school tax bill a buyer receives, and the village notes that school taxes are paid to the Town of Hempstead, not the village.

The Building Department examines and permits construction in the village and enforces the state building and fire codes plus the village code. Its FAQ lists the work that needs a permit, and several items matter to a seller who has renovated.

  • Recycling takes #1 and #2 plastics and plain brown corrugated cardboard.

How do Valley Stream village taxes work?

The village taxes about 11,000 parcels and has its own Tax Department. Village tax is due June 1 and can be paid without penalty until July 1. After that, a 5 percent penalty applies for the first month and 1 percent more each month. The village accepts no partial payments, and unpaid taxes go into the annual lien sale held the first Tuesday in May. The posted lien book was updated September 1, 2026.

The village reports an equalization rate of .87 and a residential assessment ratio of .90. Its assessment roll is final on April 1, and the grievance period opens February 1 and runs to the third Tuesday of February, when Grievance Night runs from 4 to 8 p.m. A denied complaint can go to a Small Claims petition, with the Nassau County case number obtained between April 1 and May 1.

  • Seniors 65 and over with household income under $28,900 can apply for a village exemption.
  • Veterans can receive 15 percent for wartime service plus 10 percent for combat-zone service, and Cold War veterans receive 10 percent.
  • Firefighters with more than five years of service receive 10 percent.

The senior, disability and firefighter filing window runs September 1 to December 31, so it is open now. STAR is handled by the Nassau County Department of Assessment.

How is a deed recorded in Valley Stream?

Deeds for Valley Stream property are recorded by the Nassau County Clerk in Mineola. The clerk's Land Recording Guide says to file the TP-584 transfer tax form and the RP-5217 transfer report with the deed, and a nonresident seller also files the IT-2663 estimated income tax form. Transfer and mortgage tax payments must be certified checks.

Several details reject deeds at this office: the section, block and lot numbers must appear on the first page, post office boxes are not accepted as addresses, and every signature must be original. Census Bureau data for 2020 to 2024 put the typical owner-occupied home at $616,100. The village also shows a 78.7 percent owner-occupied rate and a median gross rent of $2,124.

File between February 1 and the third Tuesday of February, when Grievance Night runs from 4 to 8 p.m. The village roll is final on April 1, and denied complaints can move to a Small Claims petition.

Where is Penfield and what does the town include?

The town lies on the eastern side of Monroe County. Webster is its northern neighbor, Perinton and Pittsford lie south, Irondequoit and Brighton west, and Walworth in Wayne County east. Its area is 37.88 square miles. Irondequoit Creek crosses the southwest corner on its way to Irondequoit Bay, which takes in part of the northwest.

Daniel Penfield bought the land in 1795, and the town was established in 1810 with mills along the creek. Six hamlets carry names today: East Penfield, Lloyd's Corners, Panorama, Penfield, Penfield Center and Roseland. Ellison Park, Veteran's Memorial Park and LaSalle's Landing Park are among its public parks. The Monroe County Sheriff's Office provides primary law enforcement, and the Penfield Fire Company covers most of the fire district while Webster's department serves the northern edge.

Students mostly attend the Penfield or Webster central school districts, and small parts of town belong to the East Rochester, Pittsford and Wayne districts. Confirm the district for a given address before advertising a house.

What do the numbers say about Penfield housing?

Penfield counted 39,438 residents in 2020 and is estimated at 39,139 for July 1, 2025, a dip of 0.9 percent. The 2020 to 2024 Census figures for housing:

  • Owner-occupied share of housing: 80.8 percent.
  • Typical owner-occupied home value: $291,500 (median).
  • Median household income: $119,154 across 15,699 households.
  • Median gross rent: $1,473.
  • Average commute: 20.0 minutes.
  • Age 65 and up: 21.3 percent of the population.

Long-time owners and a sizable senior population mean downsizing and inheritance drive many sales here. Those households often care more about a firm closing date than about staging and showings.

How does Penfield's assessment calendar work for a seller?

The town values at market. The Assessor's Office inspects from June through March 1 for new construction, additions and demolitions, and what stands on March 1 counts toward the next roll.

Penfield assessment calendar, drawn from the Assessor's Office and Board of Assessment Review pages
DateWhat happens
March 1Taxable status date. Exemption forms are due.
About May 1Notices of assessment change go out and the tentative roll is filed.
Fourth Tuesday of MayGrievance Day at Town Hall. It was May 26 in 2026, and May 25 comes next in 2027.
Before July 1Owners learn the Board's decision.
July 1Final roll filed. A 30 day window for court review begins.

The final roll feeds the school bill in September and the town and county bill the following January.

What if a Penfield owner disagrees with the assessment?

Submit form RP-524 to the Board of Assessment Review by the meeting date. The board sits in the Town Hall Auditorium at 3100 Atlantic Avenue and weighs the proof you bring, such as three or more recent sales of similar houses. A ten-minute appointment requires the original and five copies of the form and exhibits. Skipping the appointment needs the original only. Emailed or faxed forms do not replace it.

After a denial, owners who live in one-, two- or three-family homes may file a Small Claims Assessment Review petition at the Monroe County Clerk inside 30 days after the final roll. Others can bring a tax certiorari case in State Supreme Court on the same 30 day clock, and the town advises talking to a lawyer first. The board hears assessment complaints only, never complaints about the tax bill.

Which exemptions matter when a Penfield house changes hands?

An exemption covers the owner's primary home only and must be filed by March 1. The Assessor's Office lists:

  • STAR, Basic and Enhanced.
  • Limited Income Senior Citizen.
  • Persons with Disabilities and Limited Income.
  • Alternative Veteran and Cold War Veteran.
  • Agricultural Assessment.
  • Volunteer Firefighters and Ambulance Workers.

Forms go to Room 203 at 3100 Atlantic Avenue, and the staff will copy supporting papers at the counter. Renewals are mailed each fall. Someone who buys late in the year should plan to apply before the next March 1.

What permits and final sign-offs come up in a Penfield sale?

Owners need a building permit before they build, enlarge, alter, repair, move or demolish a structure, or touch electrical or plumbing systems. Sheds, barns and gazebos all require one, as do decks, hard-surface patios, finished basements and permanent standby generators. Residential fences skip the permit but face Town Code height limits: 6 feet, dropping to 3 feet within 20 feet of the front line.

The town expects each project to end with a final inspection and a Certificate of Occupancy or Compliance. Call the Building Department at (585) 340-8636 for the record on your address. Landmarks and historic districts carry extra rules, and demolishing a landmark requires a certificate of appropriateness plus a 120 day wait.

How does a Penfield deed get recorded in Monroe County?

Deeds go to the County Clerk at 39 West Main Street, Room 105, Rochester. Filing a one-page deed costs $50, with $5 for each added page. The package also needs the TP-584 ($5) and the RP-5217 ($125 for most residences, $250 otherwise), and residential deeds carry a further $10. The clerk quotes transfer tax at $4 per $1,000, the same as the state's $2 per $500. Same-day recording means standing in line by 4:30 p.m.

Unpaid taxes end up in the county's in rem foreclosure. Action No. 150 set a September 11, 2026 public auction for parcels in Penfield, Perinton, Pittsford and other towns, and that date has gone by. An owner behind on taxes can ask the County Treasury at 585-753-1200 what is owed.

What should a Penfield seller gather first?

A short folder saves days near closing:

  • Deed and any survey of the lot.
  • Permit records and the Certificate of Occupancy for decks, finished basements and additions.
  • Latest school and town and county tax bills, also viewable on the Monroe County Real Property Portal.
  • Proof of any exemption, so the buyer knows what changes after transfer.
  • Payoff figures for each mortgage or lien.

With the folder complete you can price a broker sale, a private sale and a cash offer on equal terms.

More questions about Penfield, NY

Is a sale possible with permits still open in Penfield?

Yes, though questions will follow. The Building Department wants permitted work finished with a final inspection and a certificate, and gaps can slow a sale. A cash buyer may accept the property in its current state, but the open permit remains attached to the address.

What date is Grievance Day in Penfield?

The fourth Tuesday of May. The 2026 meeting took place on May 26, and the next falls on May 25, 2027. The Assessor's Office accepts applications from May 1.

What does a typical Penfield home cost?

The 2020 to 2024 survey puts the median at $291,500 for owner-occupied homes, alongside household income of $119,154.

Does a Penfield fence need a building permit?

No, but Town Code caps fences at 6 feet and at 3 feet within 20 feet of the front property line. If a side looks better, it should face the neighbors.

Who answers Penfield assessment questions?

The Town Assessor's Office at 3100 Atlantic Avenue, reachable at (585) 340-8610 on weekdays. It sets assessments, while school, town and county tax rates come from those taxing bodies.

What should you know about selling a house in Guilderland, New York?

Guilderland is a town in Albany County that borders the city of Albany on the west, so its houses compete with the capital city's suburbs. It was part of the Manor of Rensselaerswyck from 1629, Dutch settlers began farming along the Normans Kill by the end of the 1600s, and the town was formed in 1803.

According to Wikipedia's article on Guilderland, early industry used the area's streams and forests, including a glass factory founded in 1795 around which the hamlet of Hamilton, now Guilderland, grew. The town covers about 58 square miles and its listed ZIP codes include 12084, 12085, 12009 (Altamont), 12159 (Slingerlands) and 12186 (Voorheesville).

Within the town you will find the Village of Altamont and hamlets such as Guilderland, Guilderland Center, McKownville, Westmere, Meadowdale, Fort Hunter and Hartmans Corners. Westmere sits in the eastern part of town on Route 20, McKownville is near the Albany line, and Meadowdale lies by the southern town line, so name the hamlet when you describe the house.

What do Census figures say about Guilderland housing?

Guilderland's median home value is $357,400, and only about 65 percent of occupied homes are owner-occupied, so roughly a third are rented. The Census Bureau profile gives these figures.

Guilderland town, Albany County: the Census Bureau's numbers (2025 population estimate, five-year survey data for the rest)
MeasureGuilderland
Population, July 1, 202538,216
Population change since the April 2020 base3.5%
Households14,697
Share of homes owner-lived65.3%
Typical home value$357,400

Median household income$112,273

The town grew 3.5 percent from the 2020 base to the 2025 estimate, a steady pace compared with towns that are losing residents. The renter share also means a house can attract buyers who plan to rent it out.

Which schools serve Guilderland homes?

Most of the town belongs to the Guilderland Central School District, which was formed in 1953 by merging eight smaller districts. It has one high school, Guilderland High School, one middle school, Farnsworth Middle School, and five elementary schools: Guilderland, Pine Bush, Lynnwood, Altamont and Westmere.

A few parts of the town are served by other districts, including Voorheesville Central, Schalmont Central and Mohonasen Central. Confirm the district on your tax bill, since the disclosure form has its own line for it.

What does Guilderland require for building permits?

Permits are required for most construction, renovation or structural work, and the Building / Zoning Department's FAQ gives the practical rules for sellers fixing a house before sale.

  • A complete application can take four to six weeks to approve, longer in summer.
  • All fences need a permit, and the fee depends on length. The department recommends a survey first, and it will not issue a permit over a utility easement without that agency's permission.
  • All sheds need a permit regardless of size or foundation, and sheds are allowed only in rear yards.
  • Permanent signs need a permit, but real estate for sale signs are on the list of temporary signs that do not.

The four to six week review window is the number to plan around. If a buyer's inspection turns up unpermitted work, a seller who starts the paperwork late may not finish before the contract's closing date.

How are Guilderland property tax bills paid and when do penalties start?

Town and county bills are collected without penalty in January, and school bills in September, according to the town's online tax search page. The Tax Office, in Town Hall on Western Turnpike, collects property and school taxes on about 12,500 parcels and also takes water bill payments for the Guilderland Water District.

The 2026 school tax calendar is already past its deadline. Bills were penalty-free from September 1 to September 30, 2026, a 2 percent penalty applied from October 1 to November 2, and as of November 3, 2026 unpaid school taxes are payable only to the Albany County Division of Finance. If the house you are selling still has an open balance, call the county before closing.

  • Payment options are in person, mail, a 24 hour drop box beside the Town Hall front doors, or online with a fee: $2.00 for an e-check, $4.00 for a debit card and 2.5 percent for a credit card.
  • Only a U.S. Postal Service postmark counts as proof of timely mailing.
  • The Receiver cannot waive statutory penalties, which are set by Real Property Tax Law section 924.
  • A returned check carries a $20 fee.

What can Guilderland owners do about assessments and exemptions?

The Assessor's office maintains assessments on more than 13,000 parcels and processes more than 1,000 deeds a year. It also receives copies of building permits from the Town and from the Village of Altamont, and it inspects the work to decide whether the assessment or the property inventory should change. A permitted finished basement or addition is therefore reviewed for assessment changes.

  • Informal review: submit the form and proof of value by April 1 each year.
  • Formal grievance: the town's assessment contest page lists May 25, 2027 as the last filing date for the next cycle, before 8 p.m., with an original signed RP-524 and two copies of supporting documents.
  • Exemptions: new and renewal applications are due March 1, except senior partial exemption renewals, which are due by grievance day.

Seniors, people with a physical disability and veterans may qualify for partial exemptions, per the school tax notice. If you hold one, tell your closing attorney.

How does a Guilderland deed reach the town records?

Your attorney files the deed with the Albany County Clerk, whose role the county describes as receiving, indexing, storing and retrieving documents on real property ownership. According to the town assessor's page, the county then uploads each deed and sends it to the town, and the assessor's office receives these uploads two to four times a month. A new owner's name can therefore take a few weeks to appear in town records.

Ask the Albany County Clerk for its current fee schedule, since recording charges change. Real property transfer tax follows state rules of $2 for each $500, as the Westchester County Clerk's deed guide explains, and your attorney can total the amount.

What should a Guilderland seller gather before listing or accepting a cash offer?

  • Your signed property condition disclosure statement under Real Property Law section 462, given to the buyer before any binding contract is signed.
  • Permit and certificate paperwork for any addition, deck, fence or shed.
  • The January town and county bill and the September school bill, plus the water bill from the Guilderland Water District.
  • Payoff statements, and any county tax balance.
  • A realistic closing date, given that inspections and permit reviews can each take weeks.

More questions about Guilderland, NY

Is Guilderland the same as the city of Albany?

No. Guilderland is a separate town in Albany County, west of the city. It has its own assessor, building department and tax office, and its own school district.

How long does a Guilderland building permit take?

The Building / Zoning Department says a complete application can take four to six weeks, and review can run longer in summer. Emergency repairs and demolitions may be handled sooner.

What happens to unpaid Guilderland school taxes after November 2, 2026?

As of November 3, 2026, unpaid taxes are payable only to the Albany County Division of Finance. Call the county for the amount due, including penalties, before the closing.

Do I need a permit for a for sale sign in Guilderland?

No. The town lists real estate for sale signs among the temporary signs that do not require a sign permit. Permanent signs and temporary banners do.

When are Guilderland assessment grievances due?

The town lists May 25, 2027 as the last date to file, before 8 p.m., using an original RP-524 form. Informal reviews with the Assessor are due by April 1.

How does a Clifton Park owner choose between listing and a cash sale?

A Clifton Park seller can hire an agent, handle the sale personally, or sign with a buyer who pays cash and accepts the property in its current state. The decision usually comes down to condition, timing and how much hassle you can absorb.

A listing puts your house beside every updated kitchen and fresh roof on the market, so a tired interior or an aging roof can leave a listing sitting. A cash buyer prices those flaws in and skips the open houses. You give up some of the top-end price in exchange for speed and certainty, so compare what each path leaves in your pocket after the mortgage payoff and the closing costs.

  • A listing fits a move-in-ready house and a seller with a flexible date.
  • A private sale fits an owner who has a buyer lined up and is comfortable with the contract and deed work.
  • A cash sale fits an estate house, a tired rental, a property with code issues or a job transfer that will not wait.

Where is Clifton Park, and what are buyers looking at?

Clifton Park is a suburban town in the southern part of Saratoga County, about 12 miles north of Albany, 7 miles northeast of Schenectady and 10 miles south of Saratoga Springs. The Mohawk River forms its southern boundary. The Adirondack Northway (I-87) and US Route 9 run through the eastern part, and NY Route 146 crosses the middle of town.

Growth came fast once the Northway opened in the early 1960s. The Census count went from 4,512 in 1960 to 14,867 in 1970 and 23,989 in 1980, and the town was the last one created in Saratoga County, in 1828. The area traces back to the 1707 Clifton Park Patent, and Eldert Vischer opened the Vischer Ferry crossing in 1783. The 2020 Census counted 38,029 residents and the July 2025 estimate is 37,775.

Clifton Park town, Saratoga County: Census QuickFacts, 2020-2024 estimates

Which schools and neighborhoods shape a Clifton Park sale?

Most of the town, roughly its eastern two-thirds, belongs to the Shenendehowa Central School District, while corners of the northwest and southwest fall under Burnt Hills-Ballston Lake and Niskayuna. Buyers tend to ask for the district before they ask for the square footage.

Named places inside the town include the hamlets of Rexford, Vischer Ferry, Jonesville, Elnora, Grooms Corners and Clifton Park Center, plus the neighborhoods of Clifton Knolls-Mill Creek, Clifton Gardens and Country Knolls. The town advertises a 15-mile trail network, the Clifton Common sports complex and, on the river, the Vischer Ferry Nature and Historic Preserve with a stretch of the original Erie Canal towpath. Proximity to those amenities is worth mentioning to any buyer.

Does Clifton Park charge a Town property tax?

No. The Receiver of Taxes states that the Town of Clifton Park does not have a general town tax. The January bill therefore carries County and special district charges, and school tax comes separately from whichever district serves the parcel.

A buyer comparing Saratoga County towns may care about that. Still, the total bill depends on the school district and the assessment, so hand a buyer a real bill rather than a talking point. Special districts also appear: the Receiver's office collects for the Old Nott Farm and Rivercrest Sewer Districts. School taxes are never paid at Town Hall. Shenendehowa, Niskayuna and Burnt Hills-Ballston Lake each collect their own.

When do Clifton Park tax bills arrive, and what are the penalties?

Town and County bills are mailed December 31 and are due in January. The Receiver also advises that anyone who has not received a bill by January 7 should call.

  • January: pay the exact amount on the bill with no penalty.
  • February: 1% is added.
  • March: 2% is added, plus a $2 late fee.
  • After March 31: the Receiver stops taking payment, and the Saratoga County Treasurer collects instead.

The office takes payment in person at One Town Hall Plaza, by mail to a bank lockbox in Albany, or online by card or e-check, where fees apply. The Receiver's office says the bill prints from the Assessor's records and that all changes of owner or mailing address go through the Assessor. If you sell in the fall, send the buyer's attorney your latest paid receipt so the proration at closing is clean. Escrow lenders sometimes pay the bill directly, so confirm whether yours did.

What are the Clifton Park assessment dates and exemption deadlines?

The Assessor lists March 1 as the taxable status date and the last day to file exemption applications, May 1 for the tentative roll, July 1 for the final roll, September 1 for school bills and January 1 for Town and County bills. Grievance Day is the fourth Tuesday in May.

This year's Grievance Day, May 26, 2026, has passed. The next falls on the fourth Tuesday in May 2027, which is May 25. The Town has been working to reach residents who may qualify for the senior citizen, disability and limited income, or veterans exemptions, and its 2026 notice set March 1, 2026 as the filing deadline. The assessor's office, on the second floor at 1 Town Hall Plaza, also collects data on improvements in the field and photographs them, so recent improvements may already be on record.

What local rules and offices matter when you sell in Clifton Park?

On the Town's own news page, a notice dated October 26, 2026 reports adoption of Local Law No. 14 of 2026, which amends sections 73-33 and 208-7 of the Town Code to define and regulate short-term rentals. If you planned to sell to a buyer who intends to run a short-term rental, read the adopted text at the Town Clerk's office first. Another notice from November 9 announces a hearing on a twelve-month moratorium on Tier 2 and Tier 3 solar energy applications. The same page tells residents that the last day to set out lawn and leaf bags for the Twin Bridges pickup is Sunday, November 22 by 5 p.m., which matters if you are clearing a yard before showings. It also carries a message from NYS DOT about the Adirondack Northway renewal project, worth a look for buyers who commute on I-87.

Deeds are filed with the Saratoga County Clerk at 40 McMaster Street in Ballston Spa, which accepts land recordings until 4:15 in the afternoon. The clerk's office reports digitizing more than 25 million documents. State transfer tax is $2 for each $500 of price, the seller ordinarily pays it, and Form TP-584 is filed with the clerk within 15 days after the deed is delivered. Ask the clerk for current recording fees.

Can I sell my Clifton Park house if it needs work?

Yes. A cash buyer takes houses that need updates or repairs, and the offer reflects the cost. Compare it with a listing price minus fixes, commission and carrying costs.

Who do I pay Clifton Park property taxes to?

Town and County taxes go to the Clifton Park Receiver of Taxes in January, with penalties of 1% in February and 2% plus a $2 fee in March. School taxes go to the school district, not Town Hall.

Has Clifton Park's Grievance Day already happened?

Yes. It was May 26, 2026. The next one is the fourth Tuesday in May 2027, and exemption applications are due March 1.

Does Clifton Park have its own Town tax?

No. The Receiver of Taxes states that the Town has no general town tax. County charges, special districts and school taxes still apply.

Which office files the deed after a Clifton Park closing?

The Saratoga County Clerk in Ballston Spa records it. File Form TP-584 with the deed, and ask the clerk for the latest fees.
