Is Newburgh a town or a city, and why does it matter when selling?

There are two Newburghs in Orange County, and the Census figures used on this page describe the town. The city of Newburgh, a separate municipality on the river, was part of the town until it was rechartered in 1865. Since then it has been fully independent, independent of the town.

In 2020 the town had 31,985 residents and the city and town together had 60,842. The town passed the city in population for the first time in the 2010 census. If your deed or tax bill says Newburgh, confirm which municipality issued it before you look up dates and rules.

The rest of this page covers the town: its land, its tax calendar, its school districts and the offices a seller deals with.

What is the land like in the town of Newburgh?

The town covers 43.36 square miles of land, hilly in the middle and bounded on the east by the Hudson River. Steep bluffs line most of the shoreline, so very few houses have easy river access. The northern line and about a third of the western line touch Ulster County.

Several hills top 750 feet. Cronomer Hill, at 725 feet, is the central landmark, and most of it is a county-owned park with an observation tower that looks toward the Newburgh-Beacon Bridge and Stewart Airport. On hilly lots like these, a survey and a look at drainage are worth doing before you list.

Named areas include Balmville, Gardnertown, Orange Lake, Fostertown and Algonquin Park, home to the town's only historic district built around old gunpowder mills. Newburgh is also one of eight towns in Orange County with no incorporated villages inside it.

What is the history behind the Newburgh town name and its farmland?

German Palatine refugees settled the area in 1709 under the name Neuburg, and Scottish immigrants soon joined them. The area became a precinct in 1762 and a town in 1788. When Rockland County was cut from Orange in 1798, Newburgh and other southern Ulster towns were moved into Orange County.

The town stayed rural into the twentieth century, with apple orchards in the north and dairy and vegetable farms elsewhere. The postwar years turned farmland into subdivisions and school sites. Some of that history is still visible today: the PepsiCo bottling plant stands where a Little League ballpark once did, and Wedgewood Park, planned in the 1960s, was not finished until the late 1980s.

Expect a spread of ages in the housing stock, from farmhouses to 1980s developments.

What do the roads and the airport do for house values in Newburgh?

The town calls itself the "Crossroads of the Northeast," and the map backs it up: Interstate 84 runs east to west, the New York State Thruway (I-87) runs north to south, and a direct ramp between the two opened in December 2009. Route 300 is the main commercial strip, with Routes 9W, 17K, 32, 52 and 207 also crossing the town.

Stewart International Airport sits partly in the town, though mostly in New Windsor, and much of the land around it became Stewart State Forest. Most roads are maintained by the town highway department, two are county roads, and the town also has many private roads. If your house is on a private road, ask who plows and repairs it before you list.

The Census Bureau lists 2022 retail sales per capita at $37,920 in the town, above New Rochelle ($19,931) and New Windsor ($11,352) and close to New York City ($20,303).

What do Census numbers show about Newburgh homes and buyers?

Newburgh is a town of owners, with 79.8 percent of homes owner-occupied. The Census Bureau puts the median home value at $375,700 and median gross rent at $2,159 for 2020 to 2024, which is higher rent than in New Windsor next door.

  • Households: 11,640, with 2.71 people each
  • Median household income: $111,615 in 2024 dollars
  • Poverty rate: 7.3 percent
  • Estimated population change since 2020: down 0.5 percent
  • Mean commute: 36.6 minutes

The 2022 business figures show $1,207,597,000 in retail sales, $196,134,000 in transportation and warehousing receipts and $148,831,000 in health care and social assistance revenue for the town.

Most residents have lived in the same house for years. The Census shows 93.1 percent in the same home one year earlier, so few households move in any given year.

Who bills me for taxes in Newburgh, and what are the key dates?

The Receiver of Taxes bills property tax, but school tax depends on your district, because four of them serve the town: Marlboro, Wallkill, Valley Central and the Newburgh Enlarged City School District. Who collects the school bill depends on the district:

  • Marlboro: the town Receiver collects it
  • Valley Central: the town Receiver collects it
  • Wallkill: the district's own tax collector
  • Newburgh Enlarged City School District: the district's own tax collector
DateTown of Newburgh assessment or billing step
March 1Taxable status date and exemption filing deadline
May 1Tentative roll and assessment change notices
Fourth Tuesday in MayGrievance Day
July 1Final assessment roll filed
SeptemberMarlboro and Valley Central school tax due without penalty
OctoberSame school taxes carry a 2 percent penalty
JanuaryFull property tax bill due without penalty

Source: Town of Newburgh Assessor and Receiver of Taxes pages. The town has 13,027 taxable parcels.

The Receiver does not allow partial payments or installments on property tax. Water and sewer bills come four times a year, with a 5 percent penalty after 30 days, and unpaid amounts are added to the next year's property tax bill. That last rule is worth knowing: a water balance can land on the property's next tax bill unless it is settled at closing.

What offices handle exemptions, permits and the deed?

The Assessor handles exemptions, including STAR, veterans, senior citizen, disability and agricultural ones. Ask the office which of them are on your parcel. Its page links the state's Basic and Enhanced STAR credit registration and forms for the alternative veterans, Cold War veterans, low-income disability and senior citizen exemptions. The Code Compliance Department issues building permits and certificates of occupancy for new and existing structures and investigates code complaints.

The deed itself is recorded with the Orange County Clerk, and the state transfer tax return, Form TP-584, goes to the same office within 15 days after the deed is delivered. The state tax is $2 for each $500 of price, and by default the seller pays it. The Clerk says a copy of your deed costs about $5 directly from the office, so avoid third-party companies that charge more.

When a cash buyer takes the house as-is, the same paperwork still applies. Closing the file with the clerk and settling water, sewer and tax balances is what finishes the sale.

More questions about Newburgh, NY

Is the Census population on this page for the town or the city of Newburgh?

It is for the town, which the Census Bureau estimates at 31,825 residents in 2025. The city of Newburgh is a separate municipality and is not included in that figure.

When is Grievance Day in the town of Newburgh?

The fourth Tuesday in May. The tentative roll comes out May 1, and the final roll is filed July 1.

Who collects school tax in the town of Newburgh?

It depends on the district. The town's Receiver collects for Marlboro and Valley Central, while Wallkill and the Newburgh Enlarged City School District use their own collectors.

Can I pay Newburgh property tax in installments?

No. The Receiver says installments and partial payments are not allowed for property tax, so the January amount is the full bill, and penalties start if you pay in February or March.

Do unpaid water bills affect a Newburgh house sale?

Yes. Unpaid water and sewer bills are added to the next year's property tax bill, so settle them at or before closing.

Where is Rome, and why is the city so large?

Rome sits in Oneida County in central New York and shares the Utica-Rome metro area with Utica. Its 75.7 square miles rank second among New York cities by area. With that much area, the Census Bureau's 2020 density is only 429.2 people per square mile.

Rome's 2020 population of 32,127 has slipped 1.4 percent, to an estimated 31,682. The state legislature turned the Town of Rome into a city on February 23, 1870. The city's ZIP codes include 13440, 13441 and 13442, plus 13308 for Blossvale and 13478 for Verona, so confirm the municipality on your deed and tax bill before you list.

What is Rome's history, and how does it show up in housing?

Rome grew up at the Oneida Carrying Place, an ancient portage between the Mohawk River and Wood Creek. The British built Fort Stanwix there in 1758, and the Continental forces held it through a 21-day siege in August 1777. The National Park Service rebuilt the fort between 1973 and 1976 and runs it as a museum.

Construction of the Erie Canal began in Rome on July 4, 1817, and the first cheese factory in the country opened here in 1851. Metal shops later earned the city the nickname "Copper City," with Rome turning out about 10 percent of the copper used in the United States. Griffiss Air Force Base ran from 1942 to 1995. Rome Free Academy, the public high school, moved onto former base land in 2002.

Houses of very different ages sit inside one city boundary, so a buyer's first question is usually when the house was built and what has been replaced since.

How pricey is a Rome house, and how many owners live in them?

The 2020-2024 Census Bureau survey values a typical Rome home at $154,400, and 56.6 percent of households are owners. Rent runs $909, and household income at the midpoint is $59,925.

  • 13,870 households with 2.13 people apiece
  • Residents 65 and older account for 19.8 percent
  • Poverty affects 18.1 percent of residents
  • Owner costs come to $1,431 a month with a loan and $701 with none

At that price level a major repair is a large share of a house's value, so owners sometimes weigh an as-is sale against fixing up first.

What drives the Rome economy?

Griffiss closed as a base in 1995 under the federal realignment process, but the site still houses the Rome Laboratory, now part of the Air Force Research Laboratory, and the Eastern Air Defense Sector. The old airstrip is Griffiss Airport, which has general aviation and military use but no scheduled commercial service.

Other local anchors include Rome Memorial Hospital, a 129-bed hospital, and AmeriCU Credit Union, which is headquartered in the city. In 2022 Rome's health and social-service providers took in $1.01 billion and its retailers $665 million. Workers average only 18.0 minutes to reach their jobs.

How do roads, trains and weather shape a sale in Rome?

The Utica-Rome Expressway, a 14-mile stretch of Route 49, runs from Rome to Utica, where it meets I-90 and several state routes. Routes 26, 46, 49 and 69 meet downtown. Amtrak's Empire Service stops in Rome twice a day in each direction, and CENTRO runs six bus routes in the city.

Winters are the main stress on a house here. Rome's climate table shows about 102 inches of snow in an average year and 56.7 snowy days, with January lows averaging 12.9 degrees. A tornado rated EF2 hit the center of the city on July 16, 2024, damaged roofs and brick buildings, and prompted emergency declarations from the city, county and state. If your house was damaged then, keep repair invoices and insurance paperwork together for a buyer.

Which permits does Rome require for work on a house?

Rome's Code Enforcement office issues building permits and inspects work under the state's Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code. It says to contact the office whenever you are not sure a project needs a permit.

  • Permits are generally required for new windows, kitchen and bath remodels, decks, porches and steps, pools, chimney work and any plumbing or electrical change.
  • A stop work order is issued to any job started without a permit, and fees double for work that began first.
  • Accessory structures under 144 square feet need a permit but carry no fee.
  • All plumbing must be done by a City of Rome licensed plumber.

Pools holding 24 inches of water or more need a permit, and a pool without its electrical inspection cannot get a Certificate of Compliance. Housing inspectors assigned to each ward handle property maintenance and zoning enforcement, and multiple dwellings of three units or more get fire safety and property maintenance inspections at least every three years.

When are Rome property taxes due?

Rome's city treasurer collects city, school and county taxes on a set calendar, and city taxes may include water, sewer and refuse charges. The city's printed schedule gives these dates.

The October 31 date for 2026 has passed, so the next dates are January 31 and February 28, 2027. The Treasurer's Office, in City Hall at 198 North Washington Street, can send a duplicate bill at 315-339-7689. On the assessment side, the Assessor's page lists 13,325 properties, a 2026 taxable total of $898,330,496, and grievance day on the first Tuesday in August.

What extra step does Rome add before a deed is recorded?

Rome has one extra step before the county will take a deed. The Oneida County Clerk requires the deed itself to be stamped by the Rome City Assessor first, at 198 North Washington Street, Suite 1B (315-339-7614).

The clerk's land recording page then lists a $45 statutory fee, $5 for each page, a $5 TP-584 filing fee and a $125 real property transfer report fee for residential property. A deed needs a legal description, the full names and physical addresses of both parties, and original notarized signatures. White-out or redaction means rejection. If you must correct an error, the clerk suggests drawing a new deed.

What is the fastest way to sell a Rome house?

Hiring an agent, selling on your own and taking a cash bid are the choices. With the midpoint home near $154,000, repair bills, a vacant house through a Rome winter and a sales commission each take a big bite of what you keep.

  • Choose an agent when the house shows well and you are happy to wait on a buyer's loan.
  • Choose a sale by owner if you will manage the Property Condition Disclosure Statement and the contract yourself.
  • Price out a cash bid for a home with postponed repairs, storm damage, tenants or a probate matter.

Hand the state disclosure statement to the buyer before a contract is signed. Late or missing delivery means a $500 price credit for the buyer.

More questions about Rome, NY

Does a Rome deed need a stamp from the city assessor?

Yes. The Oneida County Clerk requires deeds for Rome properties to be stamped by the Rome City Assessor before recording. Allow time for that step before closing.

Does the 2024 tornado affect how I sell a Rome house?

It can. A high-end EF2 tornado crossed the city on July 16, 2024, and damaged roofs and brick buildings. Keep repair invoices and permits to show a buyer.

Which school district serves a Rome address?

The Rome City School District covers most of the city and runs Rome Free Academy. Oriskany, Sherrill and Westmoreland districts cover other parts, so look at the tax bill.

Whom do I contact if a Rome tax bill never arrives?

Call the City Treasurer's Office at 315-339-7689 for a duplicate. Checks go to the City of Rome at 198 North Washington Street.

Is a permit required for window replacement in Rome?

Yes, generally. The Code Enforcement page lists new windows among the work that requires a permit because of energy code and egress rules, and doubled fees apply if work starts first.

Is a listing, a private sale or a cash sale best in Mamaroneck, NY?

Any of the three can work for a Mamaroneck house. The town's median owner-occupied home value is above $1 million, so a sale is a major financial decision, and some owners prefer a buyer who skips the repair list.

  • Listing: draws the most buyers, along with showings, inspection haggling and a financing contingency.
  • Private sale: you screen buyers yourself and lean on your attorney for the paperwork.
  • Cash sale: staging, fixes and open houses drop out when the buyer takes the house as it is.

One local step comes before any of these. Confirm whether your address is in the unincorporated Town, the Village of Mamaroneck or the Village of Larchmont, because the building and tax offices you deal with depend on it.

How is the Town of Mamaroneck laid out?

The Town of Mamaroneck covers 14.07 square miles in Westchester County, and 7.41 of those square miles are water, which is 52.85% of the total. Its land area is 6.65 square miles. The town contains two villages, Larchmont and the Village of Mamaroneck, though part of the Village of Mamaroneck lies in the neighboring Town of Rye. Most of the town's land is unincorporated, yet most residents live inside the villages.

Much of the unincorporated area receives mail through the Larchmont Post Office, so a Larchmont mailing address does not tell you which municipality governs the lot. The Town Center is at 740 West Boston Post Road.

The town's history shows up in sale listings and buyer questions. An Englishman named John Richbell bought the land from the Siwanoy in 1661, and the State Legislature created the town on March 7, 1788. The Mamaroneck River marks the boundary with the Town of Rye. The villages formed in the 1890s because a town could then run only elections, courts and highways, so Larchmont Manor and the harbor area incorporated to get water, sewers, sidewalks, lighting and police. Larchmont Manor had become a summer resort for New York City families, and in the early 1920s the area had a silent-film studio. Winged Foot Golf Club, which opened in 1923, hosted the U.S. Open most recently in 2020. Population grew from 29,156 in 2010 to 31,758 in 2020.

How expensive and how settled is the Mamaroneck housing market?

The middle home among owners in the Town of Mamaroneck is valued at $1,076,700, and households earn a middle figure of $163,781. Two of every three homes (66.9%) are lived in by owners. The rest of the figures here come from the Census Bureau's profile of the town.

What is the Mamaroneck calendar for contesting an assessment?

Grievances run from June 1 to the third Tuesday of June, and the 2026 window has closed. The town's key dates page sets the yearly calendar, so the next one opens June 1, 2027 and ends June 15, 2027, when the Board of Assessment Review sits.

  • May 1: taxable status date, the day ownership and condition are measured and the deadline for exemption applications.
  • June 1: the tentative roll goes online and in the office, and change-of-assessment notices are mailed to all owners, even those with no change.
  • Third Tuesday in June: the office must have every grievance in hand by then, delivered or mailed. A postmark does not rescue a late one, and email does not work.
  • September 15: the final roll appears and filing opens for Small Claims Assessment Review petitions.

The valuation date is July 1 of the prior year, so the 2026 roll reflects what a property was worth in mid-2025. The town assessor page adds that the office reviews every property transfer for accuracy, using the RP-5217 form signed at closing, and corrects the sale information it records.

Which Mamaroneck building and flood rules should a seller check?

The Town's Building and Code Enforcement department now takes permit applications online through the OpenGov Viewpoint portal, and first-time users must create an account. The department page says it issues permits for new construction, additions, alterations, plumbing, signs, erosion control and tree removal. Many jobs need a second approval from Engineering for erosion and sediment control, the Highway Department for work in the road, or the Environmental Planner for trees.

New York adopted the 2025 building standards, and work covered by the state codes after December 31, 2025 must meet them. The Town also adopted the 2020 NYStretch Energy Code and the 2025 Energy Conservation Construction Code, applying whichever provision is stricter for each component.

With more than half the town's area under water and a recorded elevation of zero feet, flood maps matter here. The department page links to the FEMA Flood Map Service Center and to FEMA's guidance on changing a flood zone. Check your parcel on the map before listing, and keep any elevation certificate nearby.

One warning from the same page applies to anyone dealing with zoning or planning matters: applicants have been the target of repeated phishing emails. The Town says it would never send correspondence from a board chairman or ask for money by wire transfer, so treat any message that does as fraudulent and call the department using the number on the Town's own site.

How much does Westchester County charge to transfer a Mamaroneck deed?

The Westchester County Clerk's fee page applies the state's $2 per $500 and shows a $404,501 purchase owing $1,620. Carried to the town's $1,076,700 midpoint, the state tax comes to roughly $4,308, and a buyer at that price would add about $10,767 in mansion tax.

A residential deed carries a $45 recording fee, $5 a page, a $5 TP-584 filing and a $125 RP-5217 filing. For a three-page deed in a single municipality the clerk shows a $190 total. The office asks filers to calculate exact amounts in its Property Records Electronic Portal, and taxes can be paid by ACH, cash, check or money order.

Once the sale closes, end your STAR registration as the state's STAR page instructs, and let the buyer register for their own credit.

More questions about Mamaroneck, NY

Is Mamaroneck a town or a village?

Both exist. The Town of Mamaroneck contains the Village of Larchmont, part of the Village of Mamaroneck and a large unincorporated area. Check which one governs your address before contacting a building or tax office.

When must a Mamaroneck grievance be filed?

By the third Tuesday of June. The 2026 window has closed, and the next one runs from June 1 to June 15, 2027. The office takes grievances in person or by mail, never by email.

Which dates set a Mamaroneck assessment?

Assessments reflect property condition and ownership on May 1, and values are based on market value on July 1 of the prior year. The 2026 roll uses mid-2025 values.

Does Mamaroneck require a permit for home work?

Yes for new construction, additions, alterations and plumbing, and the department invites owners to call if unsure. Filing happens in the online permit portal, and some projects also need engineering, highway or tree approvals.

Who pays the transfer taxes on a Mamaroneck sale?

The seller pays the state's $2 per $500 unless the contract moves it. The buyer pays the 1% mansion tax once a residential price reaches $1 million, a figure the town's midpoint home value already exceeds.

Wallkill is a town in Orange County, and it nearly encircles the city of Middletown. A separate hamlet named Wallkill sits in Ulster County, so check that any record, tax bill or listing refers to the Orange County town before you rely on it. The pieces that govern a sale here are the town Assessor and Receiver of Taxes, five different school districts, and the Orange County Clerk.

Median home value here lands well above Utica's and well below Valley Stream's. Roughly two in three housing units are owner-occupied, and workers spend about half an hour getting to work.

Where is Wallkill and what is inside the town?

The town sits near the center of Orange County. Interstate 84 crosses NY Route 17 in the southern part, and U.S. Route 6 and NY routes 17K, 211 and 302 also run through it. Neighbors include Hamptonburgh, Montgomery, Crawford, Mamakating, Mount Hope, Wawayanda and Goshen.

The land patent dates to 1724, the town was established in 1772, and during the Revolution mills in Phillipsburgh and Craigville made gunpowder for American troops. Its modern character comes from highway-era growth: the population rose from 11,518 in 1970 to 20,481 in 1980 and 30,486 in 2020, and retail is concentrated along Route 211, including the Galleria at Crystal Run. The Orange County Fair is held in the town each summer.

Which school districts bill Wallkill homeowners?

The town is split among several districts. The town's tax page lists school tax collectors for Middletown, Pine Bush, Valley Central, Goshen and Minisink, each with its own bill and website.

Collection windows differ. The Middletown district collects from October through February. Pine Bush, Valley Central, Goshen and Minisink list September and October. A seller therefore has to know which district a parcel is in, because it determines the school tax amount, the collector and the payoff. Buyers comparing schools will start from the same question, so state the district in your listing.

When are Wallkill town and county taxes due?

The Receiver of Taxes mails town and county bills around December 30, and payment is collected in three stages. The town says it handles over 10,000 bills.

  • January 1 to 31: no penalty.
  • February 1 to 28: 1 percent penalty.
  • March 1 to 31: 2 percent penalty.

No partial payments or installments are accepted, and by law the office cannot take payments after March 31. Taxes still unpaid are returned on April 1 to the Orange County Commissioner of Finance in Goshen.

A taxpayer who does not receive a bill still owes the tax and any resulting fees, according to the town page, which cites Real Property Tax Law section 992.

What does the Wallkill Assessor handle?

The Assessor keeps the roll that supports town, county, school, fire district and library taxes, and administers exemptions. The office lists STAR Basic and Enhanced, veterans, low-income senior, disability with limited income, agricultural, clergy, not-for-profit and firefighter exemptions. All exemption applications are due by March 1. A buyer who purchased after 2015 must register for STAR with the state.

To contest an assessment, file a Complaint on Real Property Assessment (RP-524) from May 1 through Grievance Day, the fourth Tuesday in May. An appointment is required, and the time is set when you file. The Board of Assessment Review sends its determinations on July 1.

The owner is responsible for keeping the mailing address, escrow account and property inventory correct. If you are selling, send the Assessor the new owner's mailing address after the deed is recorded so the next bill reaches the right person.

What will the Orange County Clerk charge for a Wallkill deed?

The Orange County Clerk records deeds for Wallkill property. Its fee list is a $45 flat fee that includes the recording page, $5 per page, $5 for the TP-584, a $10 state deed fraud letter, and $125 for the RP-5217 on a single-family or agricultural property ($250 for commercial or vacant land). The applicable transfer tax is added based on the total consideration.

Payment must be cash or check. The clerk takes no credit cards and no personal checks over $250. Checks from attorneys, title companies or other businesses over $10,000 must be certified or a money order. The Community Preservation form applies only to Warwick residents, so it will not affect a Wallkill sale.

  • Grantor and grantee names must be the same on every document.
  • The seller's signature must be notarized, and all signatures must be originals.
  • The deed needs a legal description with state, county, town and village.
  • Use black ink on white paper, with no white-out or tape.

The office examines documents for recording requirements but not for legal sufficiency, so a closing attorney should review the deed first.

What should a Wallkill seller gather before listing?

A short folder of documents saves time once an offer arrives. The town and county offices named above can supply each item.

  • The latest town and county tax bill and the school tax bill, so the buyer knows which district applies.
  • The STAR registration status, since owners who bought after 2015 register with the state.
  • Permits and certificates of occupancy for any work done on the house.
  • A copy of the current deed, which the Orange County Clerk can supply.
  • Lease copies for any tenant who will remain at closing.

With those in hand, a closing attorney can order a payoff from the Receiver of Taxes and prepare the TP-584 and RP-5217 without waiting on you.

Who handles building permits and certificates in Wallkill?

The town's Building and Code Enforcement Department is at Town Hall and keeps posted forms, including demolition application documents for 2026. If a prior owner built a deck, finished a basement or added a room, ask the department what permits and certificates of occupancy are on file for the address before you set a price.

Buyers' attorneys and lenders look for gaps between the house as built and the house as permitted, and a gap can delay a closing or push a buyer to ask for a lower price. Resolving it before you list gives you control of the timeline.

How quickly can I sell a house in Wallkill for cash?

A cash sale can close in a few weeks when title is clear. Delays usually come from estate paperwork, tenants or a missing permit, so start with those.

What does a typical house in Wallkill cost?

Census data for 2020 to 2024 show $353,200 as the middle value for owner-occupied homes, with rent around $1,790 and 64.1 percent of homes owner-occupied.

When are Wallkill town taxes due?

January 1 to 31 without penalty, with 1 percent added in February and 2 percent in March. The Receiver of Taxes cannot accept payment after March 31.

When is Grievance Day in Wallkill?

The fourth Tuesday in May. File the RP-524 complaint form from May 1 through that day, make an appointment, and expect the Board of Assessment Review's decision on July 1.

Can I pay the Orange County Clerk by credit card?

No. The clerk's deed page says recording payments must be cash or check, and personal checks over $250 are not accepted.

The town covers about 48.5 square miles, and a large swamp, Cicero Swamp, sits in its southeastern part.

The town began in 1790 as a township in the Central New York Military Tract, separated from Lysander in 1807, and lost its western half in 1827 when that portion became the town of Clay. Interstate 81, U.S. Route 11 and Routes 31 and 298 pass through, and the reconstructed Erie Canal follows the Oneida River along the north line. A small corner of Syracuse Hancock International Airport reaches the southern town line, and Michael Airfield, a single-runway general aviation field, is inside the town.

Much of the town is wetland, forest and farm land, with a growing number of housing developments pushing onto the farmland. Hamlets include Brewerton near the northern line, Bridgeport (partly in Madison County), Cicero Center on Route 31, and shoreline settlements such as Kraus Landing, Forest Beach and Lower South Bay. The Village of North Syracuse lies partly inside the town on its western edge.

Four school districts bill taxes on Cicero parcels. The town's tax receiver processes school taxes for North Syracuse Central Schools, and for the Chittenango, Central Square and East Syracuse-Minoa districts on properties in the town. Buyers will ask which district serves an address, so confirm it from the school line on the tax bill.

  • Lakeshore settlements such as Kraus Landing and Valentine's Beach sit on Oneida Lake north of Cicero Center.

How is a Cicero house assessed, and when is the next Grievance Day?

The Assessor's office values every parcel in Cicero, handles veteran, senior and disability exemptions, and tracks sales data and the equalization rate. The tentative roll was published May 1, 2026, and the town reports a 53 percent level of assessment, an equalization rate of 53 percent and a residential assessment ratio of 53 percent. A house assessed at $150,000 would therefore be viewed as having a market value of roughly $283,000 under that ratio.

The 2026 Grievance Day has already passed. The town posts the next Board of Assessment Review date as Tuesday, May 25, 2027, with hearings by appointment only at the Cicero Town Meeting Room, 8236 Brewerton Road, from 12 to 2 p.m. and 6 to 8 p.m. Complaints must be filed by 3:00 p.m. that day on form RP-524, and the town accepts them in the Town Hall drop box, by mail or by email.

  • Taxable status date is March 1, and the town page says completed exemption applications may be submitted through March 1, 2027.
  • From 2026 the State decides who qualifies for the Basic and Enhanced STAR exemptions, so questions about STAR go to the State, not the Assessor.
  • Informal reviews with the Assessor happen before Grievance Day, and the final roll is dated July 1.

When are Cicero property tax bills due?

Cicero's Receiver of Taxes processes the town and county bill, the North Syracuse village bill and the school bills. The town and county bill is mailed around January 1 and is due without penalty on February 2. School bills are mailed around September 1 and are due without penalty around October 1. Village bills (for the part of North Syracuse in town) are mailed around June 1 and due July 1.

Partial payments are accepted if nothing delinquent is owed, and the first payment must reach the office by the no-penalty date. Town and county bills can be split into up to four payments, village bills into three, and school bills into three. Mail counts as paid on its postmark date, but a postage meter mark does not count.

The tax office has one caution for sellers. It takes two to three months after a deed is filed with the county for the Assessor's records to reflect the new owner, so call the tax office when you buy or sell. Until the records change, the bill goes to the owner on file.

What do Cicero zoning and code rules mean for a seller?

The Department of Zoning and Planning issues building permits and enforces the town code from the Town Hall on Brewerton Road. A Certificate of Occupancy is issued once all work under a permit is complete and outside inspection certificates for plumbing and electrical have been received. Anything built without a permit cannot receive a Certificate of Occupancy or a Certificate of Compliance, and the town may issue a stop work order and fines.

Residents are told to find their zoning on the tax bill or the town zoning map. The office lists these permit triggers.

  • Permits are needed to add on, demolish, change occupancy, move doors and windows, repair fire damage or install a fence.
  • Fireplaces, woodstoves and heat-producing devices also need permits.
  • Ordinary repairs, siding, roofing over no more than two layers, and windows or doors of equal size need no permit.
  • A permit lasts 12 months from issue.

Plan review for a new dwelling can run two to six weeks, so an unpermitted addition is better settled before you list.

How is a deed recorded for a Cicero house in Onondaga County?

Deeds for Cicero parcels are recorded by the Onondaga County Clerk, and county records reach back to 1794. The base fee for a deed is $45.50 plus $5 per page, and transfer tax is $4 per thousand dollars of price. A TP-584 return costs $5, the RP-5217 form costs $125 for improved residential or agricultural property and $250 for improved commercial property or vacant land, and a $10 charge applies to residential deeds.

State law puts the base transfer tax on the seller, at $2 for every $500 of price, and the TP-584 is due within 15 days of the deed. Recording is also where a mansion tax of 1 percent attaches to residences at $1 million or more, and the buyer pays it. The clerk's office closes every first Tuesday of the month from 10:30 to 11:00 a.m. for a staff meeting, which is a small thing worth knowing if you are timing a closing run.

Pay the Cicero Receiver of Taxes at Town Hall, 8236 Brewerton Road, Cicero, NY 13039. The office collects town, county, village and school taxes for parcels in town.

Can I sell a Cicero house that has unpermitted work?

You can sell it, but the town cannot issue a Certificate of Occupancy or Compliance for work done without a permit. Call Zoning and Planning to learn what the town would require.

The base fee is $45.50 plus $5 per page, with $5 for the TP-584 and $125 for the RP-5217 on residential property. Transfer tax is $4 per thousand dollars of price.

Cash is attractive when a house needs updates that a mortgage lender would flag, when an estate has to settle, or when a move has a fixed date. With a median home value near $389,100, even a modest discount for a quick as-is sale adds up in dollars, so compare offers carefully.

What is Pittsford like?

Pittsford covers 23.41 square miles in the southeast of Monroe County. Mendon lies to its south, Perinton to the east, Henrietta and Brighton to the west and Brighton and Penfield to the north. The village of Pittsford was incorporated in 1827, and the Erie Canal's completion in 1825 brought mills and commerce, followed by the Auburn and Rochester Railroad in 1840. Old canal buildings along Schoen Place now hold restaurants and shops.

In 1996 the town adopted its Greenprint plan, buying development rights on roughly two-thirds of its remaining farmland, and it was the first town in New York to preserve open space that way. Eleven town parks, the Lock 32 double lock and the Erie Canal trail give the town a lot of public space, and Powder Mills and Mendon Ponds county parks lie inside its borders.

Which schools serve Pittsford homes?

The Pittsford Central School District runs two high schools, Sutherland and Mendon, plus the Barker Road and Calkins Road middle schools. Its five elementary schools are Jefferson, Park, Thornell, Mendon Center and Allen Creek. Allendale Columbia School, an independent school for nursery through grade 12, and St. Louis School are also in town, and two colleges, St. John Fisher and Nazareth, are located in Pittsford.

School reputation is a main selling point here, and buyers sometimes ask for the attendance zone of a particular address. Ask the district office to confirm the school assignment before you quote it in a listing.

What do Census figures say about Pittsford housing?

The Census Bureau counted 30,617 residents in 2020 and estimates 30,588 for July 1, 2025. For 2020 to 2024 it reports:

With so few rentals, nearly every sale involves a homeowner who has built up equity and a buyer who is moving into the district. Investor-owned houses are a small niche.

How and when are Pittsford property taxes paid?

School installments run October 15 and November 15, paid to the County Treasurer. Unpaid school balances roll onto the next year's town and county bill.

What does the assessor's calendar look like in Pittsford?

Pittsford assesses at full value and follows the state calendar. The valuation date is July 1 of the previous year, and the taxable status date is March 1, when all exemption forms must be on file. Informal reviews run from July 1 to March 1, any change is mailed between May 1 and May 15, and the formal review falls on the fourth Tuesday in May, which will be May 25, 2027.

Exemptions the Assessor's Office lists include:

  • Alternative and Cold War Veterans.
  • Volunteer firefighters and ambulance workers, worth 10 percent of assessed value.

New STAR applicants register with the State and receive a credit check instead of an exemption on the school bill. The assessor can be reached at (585) 248-6230.

What do Pittsford's code and zoning rules cover?

Pittsford requires building permits for construction, additions, alterations and demolition, pools, signs, sheds, decks, basement finishing and generators. After a permit is issued and the work meets zoning, a certificate of occupancy is issued. The Design Review and Historic Preservation Board reviews architectural plans for new structures and renovations, and the Zoning Board of Appeals hears variance requests.

Other points matter to sellers. Sewer service reaches about 70 percent of the town, so the rest use septic systems. Fences are capped at 3 feet in front of the front setback line and 6 feet behind it. Junk vehicles are prohibited, and garbage is collected by private haulers that owners hire. Parking on public highways is banned from November 15 to April 1. Code Enforcement can be reached at (585) 248-6265.

What should a Pittsford seller prepare before listing?

Pittsford buyers tend to ask detailed questions, so having answers ready helps a sale move. Consider gathering these items:

  • The deed and any lot survey, along with permits for pools, decks and finished basements.
  • Whether the house is on public sewer or a septic system.
  • Recent school and town and county tax bills, plus any exemption you currently hold.
  • The name of your private garbage hauler and any refuse district fees.

The Assessor's Property Sales Report and the Monroe County property portal give comparable sale prices for pricing the house.

How do I know if my Pittsford house is in the village?

The village of Pittsford sits in the middle of the town along routes 96 and 31, and it was incorporated separately in 1827. A house inside it may carry village charges on top of town ones, so confirm the location of your parcel. The Monroe County Real Property Portal shows tax parcel records, and the Pittsford Assessor's Office can confirm specific parcels.

County delinquent-tax foreclosure also reaches here. Monroe County's Action No. 150 covers parcels in Pittsford, including the village, and set a public auction for September 11, 2026, which has passed. Anyone behind on taxes should call the County Treasury before the next list is filed.

October 1, with full payment accepted at Town Hall through October 31 with 2 percent interest. From November 1 through 18 only the Monroe County Treasury takes payment, with 5 percent interest, and nothing is accepted after November 18.

The fourth Tuesday in May. The 2026 date was May 26, and the next is May 25, 2027. The Assessment Review Board has five members and meets once a year.

About 70 percent of the town is on community sewer service. Properties outside those areas use private septic systems, which a buyer will likely want inspected.

An average trip of 36 minutes to work is long for a city this small, and Middletown lies near the junction of I-84 and NY 17. Rent of $1,661 beside a $308,600 home value helps explain why so many houses here carry tenants. The Census QuickFacts entry for Middletown carries the rest of the figures.

What shaped Middletown, and which areas do buyers ask about?

Middletown became a village in 1848 and a city in 1888, growing around the Erie Railroad and the New York, Ontario and Western Railway. Mills here turned out shoes, lawnmower blades and furniture until industrial restructuring closed most of them by the 1960s.

Services, retail and health care carry today's economy. Large employers include SUNY Orange, the county, Orange and Rockland Utilities and Garnet Health Medical Center in the adjoining Town of Wallkill. Retail clusters along Route 211 and at the Galleria at Crystal Run to the east.

  • Presidential Heights is one of the city's more prosperous neighborhoods.
  • Highland Avenue has large Victorian houses, several now operating as nursing homes.
  • Downtown includes North and Main Streets, the Paramount Theatre and the Thrall Library.
  • Middletown Transit runs four routes from a Railroad Avenue station, and the Metro-North Port Jervis Line stop is across the line in Wallkill.

The city school district has Presidential Park, William A. Carter and Maple Hill elementary schools, Twin Towers and Monhagen middle schools, and one high school, Middletown High.

Does the Hudson Valley weather matter for an older Middletown house?

It does, because freezing winters and damp years wear on roofs, foundations and boilers. NOAA normals list a January average low of 17.8 degrees Fahrenheit, an all-time low of minus 23 and about 44.4 inches of precipitation over some 105 days each year.

Inspectors check first for stained ceilings, wet basements and old heating plants. A roof at the end of its life or a cellar that floods every spring is something a cash buyer prices in and moves past. A financed buyer may demand the fix before closing, and that costs time.

Which Middletown rental and occupancy rules affect a sale?

The rental permit is the main item. Chapter 296 of the city code forbids an owner to let anyone live in a single-family house, or an owner-occupied two-family, without a current permit from the Department of Public Works.

  • Each rental unit costs $100 to apply for, and a permit lasts two years unless the occupant changes.
  • An inspection comes before issuance and again whenever a tenant leaves and a new one arrives.
  • New tenants need a background check on file, and the managing agent must live within ten miles of the city or on site.
  • Renting without a permit carries a fine between $250 and $1,000, and each day is a separate offense.

Chapter 193 adds that a building newly built, enlarged or converted to another use may not be occupied until the Commissioner of Public Works issues a certificate of occupancy. Where a tenant lives in the house you plan to sell, confirm the permit is valid before accepting an offer. For public meetings, the Common Council sits on the first and third Tuesdays, the Planning Board on the first Wednesday and the Zoning Board on the third Wednesday.

What are Middletown's tax rates and deadlines?

City, county and library tax arrive on one bill that can be paid in two halves. March 1 is the first deadline and July 1 the second, and a 2 percent penalty lands the next day.

Rates posted for January 1, 2026, stated per $1,000 of assessed value, are $100.4323 city, $22.890301 county and $6.426390 library, which adds up to $129.75. After the penalty, 1 percent monthly interest starts April 1 on the first half and August 1 on the second.

The assessment calendar starts March 1, which is both taxable status date and exemption deadline, then adds the May 1 tentative roll, a Grievance Day on the fourth Tuesday of May, and a final roll on July 1. The Assessor also checks each transfer for buyer, seller and price.

Neglected houses carry one more risk. Under a local law in effect since 2024, the city can move unpaid charges for tall grass, snow removal, garbage cans, bulk pickup, dead trees and demolition onto the property tax bill. Settle any open charges with the Finance Office before closing, and see the city's Taxes page for the notice.

What does recording a Middletown deed involve?

The Orange County Clerk records the deed. According to the clerk's Deeds page, a residential filing pays $125 for the RP-5217 and a flat $45 that covers the recording page, then adds a per-page charge of $5, a $5 TP-584 fee and a $10 state deed fraud letter.

Payment comes by cash, check or money order, and checks are written to the Orange County Clerk. Personal checks are capped at $250, and cards are not taken. Signatures on the deed must be originals with a notary's acknowledgment, and clerks review the form for recording requirements without ruling on legal sufficiency.

Sellers owe the base transfer tax, and the Department of Taxation and Finance sets the return deadline at the 15th day after the deed is delivered. The extra levies that page lists for New York City never touch a Middletown closing.

More questions about Middletown, NY

Can a Middletown house with tenants be sold?

Yes, provided the rental permit is current. The city demands one for single-family and owner-occupied two-family rentals, and it names the tenant. Call the Department of Public Works to check the status before taking an offer.

What is the combined Middletown tax rate?

It is $129.75 per $1,000 of assessed value as of January 1, 2026, made up of $100.4323 city, $22.890301 county and $6.426390 library. Bills fall due March 1 and July 1.

What date is Grievance Day in Middletown?

It lands on the fourth Tuesday in May, after the May 1 tentative roll. Exemption applications close March 1.

What does the Orange County Clerk charge to record a deed?

A residential deed costs a flat $45 plus $5 per page, with separate charges for the TP-584, the deed fraud letter and the $125 RP-5217, and transfer tax on top. Check the clerk's Deeds page before filing.

Are New York City transfer taxes charged on a Middletown sale?

No, those taxes apply to conveyances inside New York City. A Middletown seller pays the standard state rate of $2 per $500.

Which options exist for a fast North Tonawanda sale?

In North Tonawanda you can list with an agent, sell on your own, or accept a direct cash purchase, and the choice usually turns on the condition of the house and how long you can wait. Start by confirming your address is inside the city, because the 14120 ZIP code also covers southern parts of the towns of Wheatfield and Pendleton.

North Tonawanda is a city of about 10.9 square miles in Niagara County, bounded by the Niagara River on the west and Tonawanda Creek and the Erie Canal on the south. The Census Bureau estimated 29,806 residents on July 1, 2025, down 2.3% from the 2020 base. It is the second-largest city in the county after Niagara Falls. Across the canal lie the City of Tonawanda and the Town of Amherst in Erie County, and the Town of Wheatfield borders North Tonawanda on the north and east.

  • Median value of an owner-occupied home, 2020 to 2024: $197,200
  • Owner-occupied housing rate: 70.1%
  • Median gross rent: $934 a month
  • Median household income: $66,961
  • Residents 65 and older: 21.9%
  • Persons in poverty: 12.4%

With 14,015 households averaging 2.14 people, North Tonawanda skews toward long-time owners. About 91% of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, which points to a settled owner base.

What is North Tonawanda known for, and who buys houses here?

The city calls itself the Lumber City, and its housing grew out of that history. From the mid-19th century into the 1970s it was a lumber forwarding center and, at the height of the Erie Canal, the largest port on the Great Lakes. More than 150 lumber companies operated here, and the Ray H. Bennett Lumber Company sold kit homes across the United States and Canada for about 70 years.

It is also the birthplace of the Herschell carrousel company, and the Herschell Carrousel Factory Museum is on Thompson Street. Wurlitzer took over the band organ factory in 1909, and the old Wurlitzer plant now holds light industrial and commercial tenants. Goundry Street has mansions built for lumber barons, including Kent Place at 208 Goundry Street.

The city became a village in 1865 and was incorporated as a city on April 24, 1897. Downtown draws buyers who like the Riviera Theatre on Webster Street, the City Market that opened in 1908, Gateway Harbor Park on the canal, and Gratwick-Riverside Park, a 53-acre park on the Niagara River. The arts scene downtown also includes the Ghostlight Theatre, the Carnegie Art Center in the former Carnegie Library and the Railroad Museum of the Niagara Frontier in a 1923 Erie Railroad station.

Do North Tonawanda rental properties have to be registered?

Yes. Under Chapter 51D of the city code, every owner of rental property in North Tonawanda registers each rental unit with the Building Department, and owner-occupied properties register too, without a fee.

North Tonawanda rental registration, yearly fee (City Rental Unit Registration page)
PropertyFee
1 to 3 dwelling units$35 per unit
4 or more dwelling units$140
Owner-occupiedNo fee, registration still required

A certificate is valid up to one year or until ownership changes, so the buyer of a rental house registers in their own name after the deed transfers. Registering consents to inspection by Code Enforcement for compliance with the city chapter and the New York State building and fire codes.

  • Applicants submit photo identification.
  • An owner who does not live in Niagara County, Erie, Genesee or Orleans County must name a property manager who does, and who can accept legal notices.
  • A first conviction for failing to register carries a fine of $250 to $500. A second within twelve months carries $500 to $2,500.
  • A fine unpaid after 30 days becomes a lien on the property and is collected like a tax.

If you own a rental, clear any registration gap before you sell, since a lien would surface in a title search. The Building Department number on the registration page is (716) 692-2680, and the office is at 216 Payne Avenue.

When can you grieve your North Tonawanda assessment?

Grievance Day is always the fourth Tuesday in May, and the Assessor's office has the forms starting in March. The assessor's page also carries the 2026 final roll and a property search where you can open any parcel and select Additional Info, then View Tax Detail, to see a tax summary by year.

The same office lists the exemptions a buyer may ask about:

  • Basic STAR requires owning and living in the home with 2024 income of $500,000 or less.
  • Enhanced STAR requires age 65 by the end of 2026 and 2024 adjusted gross income of $110,750 or less.
  • People who bought after 2015 sign up with the state for the STAR Credit.
  • The low-income senior exemption has a 2025 income limit of $34,400, and the disability exemption has a limit of $34,600.
  • Veterans exemptions are capped for assessments above $120,000.

The Assessor will give you a free copy of your deed on request, which helps when you are assembling closing papers. Contact the office at 695-8597 for details.

How are deeds filed and transfer tax paid in North Tonawanda?

Deeds for a North Tonawanda sale go to the Niagara County Clerk, not City Hall. The Assessor's page points filers to the clerk's deed recording office at (716) 439-7022, with recording hours of 9:30 AM to 4:30 PM on weekdays.

The county clerk requires the signed original deed plus a TP-584 transfer tax return and an RP-5217 real property transfer report. The seller pays the state transfer tax of $2 for each $500, or $4 per $1,000, and the state sets the filing deadline at 15 days after the deed is delivered. A closing attorney or title company normally handles this for you.

Before closing, settle city water. The Clerk/Treasurer's office warns that after two consecutive estimated water meter readings, a $25 fee applies each quarter until the meter is read, and meter readings can be dropped off or submitted online. Ask the Treasurer's office at (716) 695-8575 for the current balance and how it is handled at transfer.

What are the schools, roads and climate like in North Tonawanda?

The North Tonawanda City School District runs North Tonawanda High School, North Tonawanda Middle School, Drake Elementary, North Tonawanda Intermediate School, Spruce Elementary and Ohio Elementary. The Census Bureau reports that 94.0% of adults 25 and older finished high school and 27.1% hold a bachelor's degree or higher.

Niagara Falls Boulevard, which is US Route 62, marks the northeastern boundary, the Erie Canal runs along the south and much of the east, and Tonawanda Island at the southwest corner belongs to the city. The mean commute is 20.4 minutes. Precipitation falls on about 171 days a year here, and snow on about 57 days, according to NOAA normals reported on Wikipedia, so roof, gutter and basement condition deserve a close look before you list.

More questions about North Tonawanda, NY

Can I sell a rental house in North Tonawanda if it is not registered?

Register it before the sale. Failing to register is a violation with fines of $250 to $500 for a first conviction, and an unpaid fine becomes a lien on the property.

Where do I file a deed after selling in North Tonawanda?

File it with the Niagara County Clerk. The seller pays transfer tax of $2 per $500, and the TP-584 and RP-5217 forms go in with the deed.

When is Grievance Day in North Tonawanda?

It is always the fourth Tuesday in May. Grievance forms are available from the Assessor's office starting in March.

Is a 14120 mailing address always inside North Tonawanda city limits?

No. The ZIP code 14120 also covers southern parts of the towns of Wheatfield and Pendleton, so check your tax bill to see which municipality governs your house.

What happens to my rental registration when I sell?

The certificate lasts up to one year or until ownership changes. After the sale the new owner registers the units with the Building Department.

Selling in Glenville?

Taxes on the sale itself

What should a Glenville seller know before choosing how to sell?

A Glenville owner can list with an agent, sell privately, or accept a cash offer, and each route changes how fast the sale closes and what the house must look like. Glenville is a town in Schenectady County that was incorporated in 1821, and it takes in the part of the county north of the Mohawk River, including the Village of Scotia.

The town is largely a bedroom community. Wikipedia's summary of Glenville notes that many residents work at General Electric in Schenectady, in state offices in Albany, or at other Capital District employers. That commuter pull is why a Glenville house often sells on location, school district and drive time rather than on its finishes alone.

The town is spread over several named areas: Scotia in the south, Alplaus in the east, Hoffmans along Route 5, West Glenville in the northwest, and East Glenville along NY-50. Stoodley Corners, at Route 50 and Glenridge Road, is the commercial core people call Town Center. Buyers, and cash buyers, price each area differently, so say which one your house sits in when you ask for offers.

What do the Census numbers say about housing in Glenville?

Glenville is mostly owner-occupied, with a median home value in the mid $250,000s. The table below pulls the housing lines from the Census Bureau's town profile.

Glenville town, Schenectady County: what the Census Bureau reports (housing lines are five-year survey figures)
MeasureGlenville

Three of those lines matter to a seller. About 91 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, so turnover is low and a listing stands out. The owner rate means most nearby buyers are households that will want a mortgage-friendly condition. The commute figure matches the town's role as a suburb of Schenectady and Albany.

Which sale route suits a Glenville house in rough shape?

A house with deferred repairs usually fits a cash sale or a discounted as-is listing better than a full retail listing. A retail listing works best when the roof, systems and cosmetics will pass a buyer's inspection and a lender's appraisal.

  • Agent listing: the widest buyer pool, but you carry showings, repairs requested after inspection, and a closing that can slip if the buyer's loan stalls.
  • Private sale: you keep the commission line, but you handle pricing, paperwork and negotiation yourself.
  • Cash offer as-is: fewer contingencies and a closing date you pick, usually at a lower price than a repaired and staged listing.

Whatever route you take, New York's Real Property Law section 462 requires a seller of a one to four family home to give the buyer a signed property condition disclosure statement ahead of the buyer's signature on a binding contract. The same section confirms the parties may still agree to sell the property as is. The form asks about flood zones, wetlands, fuel tanks, radon tests, roof age, sump pumps and the septic or sewer system, so gather those answers early.

Do Glenville building rules affect the sale?

Yes, because open or unfinished work can stall a buyer's lender or a title search. The Town of Glenville Building Department, in the Municipal Center on Glenridge Road, says a permit is required for new construction, additions, structural changes, decks, fences, finished basements, conversions, swimming pools, demolition, roofing, siding and new windows and doors.

Its application page asks owners to plan on about 10 days for most permit reviews. If you finished a basement or put up a deck without a permit, ask the department what it needs before you list, because a buyer's attorney can raise it at contract.

  • The town page on swimming pools says any pool that can hold more than 24 inches of water needs a permit and a final inspection before use, including inflatable and quick-set pools.
  • Homes inside the Village of Scotia may deal with the village's own building office, which the town's department list points to separately.
  • The Glenville Town Court page lists summary proceedings, which is where a landlord's eviction case would be heard if a tenant occupies the house.

How do Glenville property tax bills work when a house sells?

Glenville has two tax cycles, and the closing attorney will split each between you and the buyer. The town's About Your Taxes page says town and county bills usually go out by January 1 and are due without penalty by the end of January. The collection window runs through April with a penalty each month on the bill: 1.25 percent in February, 2.5 percent in March and 3.75 percent in April. On May 1 the unpaid balance moves to the Schenectady County Commissioner of Finance.

School bills are mailed by about September 1, are due without penalty by the end of September, and pass to the county on November 1 if unpaid. An unpaid school bill with penalties is added to the next January town and county bill, so a skipped school payment shows up on a bill the buyer would otherwise expect to be clean. Water rent bills go out by June 1 and unpaid water charges are also carried onto the following January bill.

The same page explains the bill's line items. County and town general charges apply to every parcel in town. Town outside, highway and some other lines apply only to parcels outside the village. Fire district and special district charges depend on the street. A house in Scotia also receives a separate village bill, due in June.

How can a Glenville owner challenge an assessment or use exemptions before selling?

A lower assessment helps only if you file before grievance day, which in Glenville is the fourth Tuesday in May. The Assessor's Office page lists that date in its hours, and the town's assessment dispute page links the state RP-524 complaint form and its instructions.

The Assessor's Office also handles exemptions. The town's department menu lists separate pages for veterans, low-income seniors, and volunteer firefighters and ambulance workers, plus a page on the STAR program. If you receive STAR on the house, tell your closing attorney, because the benefit is tied to the owner. The state's STAR registration page tells a seller to close the registration after a sale and tells a new owner to register once the house becomes their primary home.

What happens with Glenville water and sewer at closing?

Glenville runs an online request just for sellers. The Public Works water and sewer pages include a Closing Adjustment Request form, and the form page asks you to allow 48 hours for the water or sewer closing adjustment to be forwarded to the closing contact. File it as soon as you have a contract date so the buyer's attorney is not waiting on a meter reading.

If the house is on a private well or septic system rather than town service, the disclosure statement still asks about water source, water testing, sewage type, and the date a septic tank was last pumped. A cash buyer will usually ask for the same details.

How does a Glenville deed get recorded?

The deed is recorded with the Schenectady County Clerk, and the county then passes the ownership change to the town. The town's assessor page explains that counties process deed transactions and send them on to towns for data entry, and it links a search of Schenectady County deeds.

The paperwork around a deed follows New York's standard package. The Westchester County Clerk's deed recording guide shows the usual pieces: form TP-584 and the Real Property Transfer Report RP-5217, plus state transfer tax of $2 for each $500 of price. Fees differ by county, so ask the Schenectady County Clerk for its current schedule, or ask your closing attorney to quote the total.

  • Confirm the legal owners on the deed match the people signing the contract.
  • Collect any open permit paperwork before the attorney orders the title search.
  • Ask the attorney for the final figure for transfer tax and recording fees in writing.

What should you compare before accepting a Glenville offer?

  • The net amount after taxes, payoffs, water charges and recording costs, not just the headline price.
  • Whether the buyer takes the house as is, or asks you to complete repairs after inspection.
  • The closing date, and who covers any gap between contract and closing.
  • Proof of funds, if the offer is cash.
  • Any condition tied to the disclosure statement or a title problem.

More questions about Glenville, NY

Can I sell a Glenville house without making repairs first?

Yes. New York law lets a seller and buyer agree to an as-is sale, but you must still give the buyer a signed property condition disclosure statement ahead of the buyer's signature on a binding contract. Expect an as-is price to sit below a repaired, staged listing.

Who do I pay property taxes to in Glenville?

Town and county bills are paid to the Glenville Receiver of Taxes in January, with monthly penalties through April. School bills are collected in September. After the deadlines pass, unpaid bills move to the Schenectady County Commissioner of Finance.

Does a Scotia address change anything about the sale?

It can. Houses inside the Village of Scotia receive a village tax bill due in June, and the village has its own building office. Houses elsewhere in Glenville do not get that bill.

How do I get the water and sewer figures for my closing?

Submit the closing adjustment request on the town's Public Works water and sewer pages and allow 48 hours. The result goes to the closing contact you name on the form.

When is grievance day in Glenville?

It is the fourth Tuesday in May, according to the Assessor's Office hours. File the state RP-524 form before then if you think your assessment is too high.

Gates owners can hire an agent, go it alone, or take a cash offer from someone who buys the house as it stands. Gates is a town in Monroe County and a suburb of Rochester, so the town hall, the Monroe County Clerk and the county's tax portal handle most of the paperwork.

A fast sale mostly depends on having clean records. In Gates that means a current Compliance Certificate for any work done, a tax payoff figure and the right school district named on the bill.

What does the Census say about work and commuting in Gates?

Gates residents commute an average of 17.5 minutes, and 62.7% of people 16 and older are in the labor force. Some 92.3% of adults 25 and older finished high school and 28.5% hold a bachelor's degree or higher.

The town's economic base shows up in the 2022 receipts: transportation and warehousing at about $194 million, health care and social assistance at about $138 million, and retail sales at about $556 million. Those numbers sit alongside the Wegmans headquarters and Rochester Tech Park, both inside the town.

Median household income is $77,080, and about 11% of residents are in poverty. Ask your agent or lender how an appraisal could affect a financed buyer before you accept an offer.

Where is Gates and how did it develop?

Gates sits in central Monroe County and borders the city of Rochester on its east side. It spans about 15.3 square miles, and the geographic center of Monroe County falls inside the town. Interstate 390 curves through the east, Interstate 490 crosses the middle, and Route 531 runs northwest toward Spencerport.

The area was organized in 1797 as Northampton in Ontario County. In 1808 the remaining portion was renamed Gates, after General Horatio Gates, and the town was incorporated on April 1, 1813. Monroe County was created in 1821. Parts of the old town later went to the city of Rochester and the Town of Greece.

  • Employers: Wegmans Food Markets keeps its headquarters in Gates, and Rochester Tech Park occupies a former Kodak plant site.
  • Zip codes: 14624 and 14606 cover most of the town, and a part falls under Spencerport's 14559.
  • Schools: the Gates-Chili and Spencerport school districts both draw on Gates property.

How did the 2025 reassessment change things for Gates sellers?

The Town of Gates states that it completed a town-wide reassessment in 2025, and the Assessor's page now lists a 2026 final tax assessment roll. For a seller, that means the assessed value printed on a tax bill is recent and tied to current market value.

The assessor's office compares each property to nearby sales and adjusts values when a building permit shows new construction, remodeling or demolition. The assessment funds the town, Monroe County, the school district and special district charges such as the fire and ambulance districts.

The assessment calendar runs on a fixed cycle:

  • March 1: taxable status date, and the exemption filing deadline.
  • May 1: tentative roll filed and grievance forms become available.
  • Fourth Tuesday in May: Grievance Day before the Board of Assessment Review, which has five resident members.
  • July 1: final roll filed, with decisions mailed by that date.

How are Gates property taxes billed and paid?

Gates owners receive two bills a year. The Town and County bill covers a calendar year and the school bill covers July 1 to June 30. The Tax Receiver's office is at 1605 Buffalo Road, and the town's page lists the interest schedule.

Because penalties rise month by month, a seller who is behind should get a written payoff figure before setting a closing date. After May 31, collection moves to the Monroe County Treasurer.

  • Town and County bill: mailed around the turn of the year, with full payment due by February 10 to avoid interest.
  • Late rates: interest begins at 1.5% from February 11 and climbs to 6% by May.
  • School bill: mailed so it arrives in early September, with full payment due by October 1.

Which town services and records are useful to a Gates seller?

The Town of Gates website carries most of the forms you may need while preparing a sale, and its Town Code is posted online. The Tax Receiver's office accepts cash, check and card, though a card payment adds a fee, and the town cautions that bill pay can take up to 14 days and arrive without a postmark.

  • Code complaints: the town accepts a code or dog complaint through an online form.
  • Electrical work: the town keeps a list of approved electrical inspectors, which helps if a buyer wants electrical work signed off.
  • Yard debris: a pickup schedule is posted online, and a refuse hauler list is available.
  • Fire and ambulance: special district charges for the Gates Fire Department and Gates Volunteer Ambulance are based on assessed value.

The Board of Assessment Review can only hear valuation complaints, not tax complaints, so a seller who thinks the bill is wrong should first check whether the assessed value or an exemption is at issue.

What permits and recording steps apply to a Gates sale?

The Gates Building Department reviews plans, issues permits for decks, pools, additions and signs, and issues Compliance Certificates. Zoning questions go to the same office, and a Zoning Compliance Request carries a $75 fee. The Zoning Board of Appeals meets the second Monday of each month for variance requests.

After closing, the deed is recorded by the Monroe County Clerk, who acts as registrar of deeds and mortgages, at 39 W. Main Street, Room 101 in Rochester. New York charges a seller's transfer tax of $2 per $500 of price, and the TP-584 form goes in with the deed. The Monroe County Real Property Portal shows tax bills and sales histories for parcels.

Ask the Building Department for a printout of permits on the parcel, and confirm that the Assessor's records match the house as it stands today.

More questions about Gates, NY

What is a Compliance Certificate in Gates?

It is a document the town Building Department issues after required permits and inspections are complete. Buyers' attorneys often ask for it when a seller added a deck, pool or alteration, so confirm yours is on file.

When is the Gates tax bill due without interest?

Full payment of the Town and County bill is due by February 10. Interest begins on February 11 at 1.5% and rises through May, and payments after May 31 go to the Monroe County Treasurer.

Which school district is my Gates house in?

Gates property falls within either the Gates-Chili Central School District or the Spencerport Central School District. Your tax bill names the district, and the Assessor's Office can confirm it.

Can I challenge my Gates assessment after the 2025 reassessment?

Yes. File the grievance form with the Assessor by the fourth Tuesday in May, and the Board of Assessment Review decides by July 1. Bring sales of similar nearby homes as evidence.

Where is the deed recorded for a Gates house?

At the Monroe County Clerk's office in downtown Rochester, which keeps deeds, mortgages and liens. The office keeps weekday hours from nine to five.

Where is Chili, NY, and what kind of town is it?

Chili is a suburban town in the southwest corner of Monroe County, and its northeastern corner touches the city of Rochester. The town was cut from Riga on February 22, 1822, and it covers about 39.9 square miles, almost all of it land. Downtown Rochester sits roughly 7 miles northeast of the hamlet of Chili Center.

Both Interstate 490 and the New York State Thruway cross the town. The town's own communities include Chili Center, North Chili (home to Roberts Wesleyan University), South Chili along the Thruway, West Chili near Black Creek Park, and the rural hamlet of Clifton. Black Creek Park runs nature trails along the creek, and the Genesee River forms part of the eastern edge.
